title: How to Use Docker in this Class
text:
By completing this guide, you will

have access to Docker Desktop on your computer,
understand how to use the class Docker image (or Dockerfile) to create a container with persistent storage, and
have access to a standardized computing environment.

title: How to Use Docker in this Class
text:
What is Docker?
Docker is a collection of technologies that allow developers to run applications in isolated environments. For example, a company like Netflix might use multiple containers to isolate different parts of the user experience (logging in to your account, billing, selecting a series to binge). In the realm of data analysis, researchers and analysts use Docker to package fragile software stacks, such as a specific version of Julia, Python, or R combined with custom libraries and GPU drivers, so that data processing, modeling, and other pipelines can be shared and run anywhere without breaking. In either setting, careful management of the computing environments under which discrete tasks are carried out is a central concern.

title: How to Use Docker in this Class
text:
Why are we using Docker?
While there are many ways in which containers might be applied, our interest in isolated environments is motivated by the following:

Standarization and Consistency. Everyone in the class will run the same OS, the same system dependencies, and identical software versions.
Minimal Installation Friction. There is a benefit to learning how to manage systems on your own, from scratch, as you build out your workspace and tools. Unfortunately, the quarter system does not allow much time for exploration, experimentation, and failure. Most of the hard work has been handled by building the class Docker image.
Reproducbility. Containerization helps us practice reproducbility in our work. It makes for good science, good software, and excellent communication of your work.

title: How to Use Docker in this Class
section: So how do I use it?
text:
So how do I use it?
There are few terms we need to define before we use Docker.

Dockerfile: This is a recipe that defines an environment. It’s just a text file with Bash commands (usually) and some additional Docker-specific syntax.
Image: This is the product generated by running the recipe in a Dockerfile. It is a read-only environment, configured with a specific Operating System (OS), file structure, and accompanying software.
Container: Whereas images are static, containers are dynamic. It is the “runtime” or how we use a Docker image. A single image can be used to spin up multiple containers, each running instances of the same or related applications. The environment is the same each time you create a container, from scratch, using the same image.
Volume: You can create and destroy data within a container, but Docker containers are deliberately disposable. A (storage) volume allows you to persist data after you shut down a container. This works by mapping data (files, folders, programs, etc) from a container to your disk.
Docker Desktop: The main software from Docker that we will use, which handles building images, container creation, and deployment.


1. Download and Install Docker Desktop
Point your preferred web browser to https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/ and select the appropriate download for your OS and architecture.






WarningWindows Users




If you have a Surface or Copilot+ laptop, it has a Qualcomm Snapdragon CPU. Select the ARM64 option.
Otherwise, you have an Intel or AMD CPU. Select the AMD64 option.



Follow instructions from the installer.


2. Download our docker-compose.yml

This is a file to automatically construct a container from pre-built images.
Please download it from Canvas.
Be sure to download it to a convenient location where you would like to store your course materials.







WarningWindows Users



Avoid placing your course materials, including docker-compose.yml, inside a folder that is backed up by cloud services like OneDrive or Google Drive. The automated nature of such tools risk corrupting your files if a backup triggers while your container is running, resulting in data loss.
Suggested Workaround: Store your work directly under your C:\ drive; for example C:\STAT206.




3. Create your local container
First, open the terminal view in Docker Desktop.





Next, navigate to the folder/directory containing the docker-compose.yml file. Once you’ve verified the file’s presence, enter and run the command docker compose up -d stat.





The Containers tab in Docker Desktop shows the status of your container.






Gray circle: Not running
Green circle: Running (in the background)
You can start/stop the container using the Play/Stop button under Actions.

The docker ps command can also be used to monitor your container from a CLI.







4. Using the Container
If you want to access the container from your machine’s Terminal:
docker start -ai STAT206-STAT

docker start: The start action will only start an existing container.
-ai: The option a ensures we can see messages in our terminal and propagates signals (such as force quitting). The option i is used to indicate an interactive session.
STAT206-STAT the name of the container we wish to run.

If you just want the container to run in the background so you can connect to it using VSCode:
docker start STAT206-STAT
You can stop a running container using:
docker stop STAT206-STAT

title: How to Use VSCode with a Container
text:
Basic Setup

1. Install the Dev Containers Extension
In VSCode, navigate to the Extensions menu and install the Dev Containers extension.







2. Make sure a container based on the class image is running.

From a terminal, run docker start STAT206-STAT.
From Docker Desktop, open the dashboard and navigate to Containers. Click on the Run button for STAT206-STAT.



3. Attach a VSCode window to the container
Open the Command Palette and select Dev Containers: Attach to Running Containers... and wait for the connection.






Windows: Ctrl + Shift + P
MacOS: Ctrl + Shift + P

Now VSCode can interact with the file system on the container. In the future, you only need to attach VSCode to the container.

title: How to Use VSCode with a Container
text:
Manipulating files through VSCode
The File Explorer allows you to explore directories and view files.






Windows: Ctrl + Shift + E
Linux/MacOS: Ctrl + Shift + E

There are New File and New Folder buttons that appears in the top right-hand corner of the File Explorer when hovering your cursor.










Opening a file allows you to edit its contents like any other text editor. The Extensions feature in VSCode can modify the editor to provide additional support for specific file types.

To upload a file or directory to the container, you can drag and drop it onto the File Explorer.

After reading this guide, you should

be able to create commits signed with your chosen username and email,

understand how to set up Git on a computer.

title: Configure Git
text:
Overview
We will use Git for version control of our work throughout the quarter. You will spend most of your time working in a single-user setting, editing and managing your own repository for assignments. Later in the course you will work in a small team and use Git to coordinate development.
Before that can happen, we’ll need to configure Git.






NoteConfiguration Files



Dr. Landeros prefers to use a ~/.config/ directory to store configuration files as much as possible. This practice is based on the XDG Base Directory Specification, which a tool like Git respects. That said, not every tool across Linux distributions will adhere to this standard.

title: Configure Git
text:
Method 1: Quick and easy
The following commands will create a global configuration file at ~/.gitconfig.
git config --global user.name "CHOSE YOUR NAME"
git config --global user.email "UCR EMAIL"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"

title: Configure Git
text:
Method 2: Using an editor

Create and open a file: ~/.config/git/config. Alternatively, you may use a file at ~/.gitconfig. Just choose whichever approach appeals to you.
In the file, type in the following information (mind the indentation):
[user]
    name = CHOOSE YOUR NAME
    email = UCR EMAIL
[core]
    editor = code --wait

title: Configure Git
section: What does the core.editor option do?
text:
What does the core.editor option do?
If you run git commit in a Git repository, the command set for core.editor is run automatically for you. This is convenient for quickly drafting a commit message.
Alternatively, you can use the VSCode interface for writing commits.

title: Configure Git
text:
Check your work

Read the contents of ~/.config/git/config
Check the output of git config --global --list.
Check the output of git config --global --list --show-source.

title: Configure Git
text:
Optional: Address colorblindness
By default, the command git diff relies on red (for deletions) and green (for additions) to highlight changes in files. Other Git commands use red and green to tag the state of varies files in a repository. Fortunately, the tool can be configured to use colorblind-friendly alternatives and increase its accessibility.

Option 1: Change the diff colors
In a command line:
git config --global color.diff.old "yellow"
git config --global color.diff.new "blue"
Alternatively, edit your Git configuration file:
[color "diff"]
    old = yellow
    new = blue


Option 2: Disable color-coded output
In a command line:
git config --global color.ui false
Alternatively, edit your Git configuration file:
[color]
    ui = false

title: Control Flow
text: Goals

title: Control Flow
text:
Overview
Literals, variables, and built-in/package functions are quite useful but insufficient for writing complex scripts and programs. Here we briefly review syntax for conditional statements and repeated evaluation. These two concepts vastly increase the expressiveness of any programming language. We then shift our attention to user-defined functions, highlighting scoping rules and other features in Julia.

title: Control Flow
text:
Conditional Statements
Conditional statements allow a program to change its behavior based on some state, usually captured by one or more variables.

if condition1
  # do something
elseif condition2
  # do something
else
  # do something
end

Here, condition1 and condition2 must be Julia expressions that evaluate to true or false. There are a few points to be aware of:

Most programming languages treat true and false as 1 and 0 (integers). This is true in Julia, but the reverse is not allowed.
Julia uses the Missing type to represent missingness, and Nothing to represent void. The former can appear as the result of a Boolean expression. The proper way to check for missingness or nothingness is to use ismissing() or isnothing(), respectively.
Conditional statements can be chained and nested.
Whitespace does not have special meaning in Julia. Thus, it is perfectly acceptable to write
The order in which you check conditions matters!


if condition something end







Important



Every conditional statement introduces a branch in your code. Excessive branching may obscure intended meaning and potentially slow down your code.



Example: Checking for an empty collection

mydata = Int[] # array of Ints
if isempty(mydata)
  push!(mydata, 100)
else
  mydata[1] = 100
end

The cell above displays an array with 1 element.

Which branch was executed?
Why do we see any return value at all?



Example: A biased coin flip

u = rand()
if u < 1/3
  println("Heads")
else
  println("Tails")
end

The code above behaves randomly because the printed message depends on the value of u.

What is the probability of seeing the outcome "Tails"?
Justify your answer to the question above.
What about the probability of seeing "heads"?



Shorthand: Elvis Operator
Like other languages, Julia supports the “ternary” operator ?:, sometimes referred to as the Elvis operator. It is shorthand for if-else, but it can be chained to mimic if-elseif-else (don’t do that!).

condition1 ? alternativeA : alternativeB



Example: Writing a quick message

mymood = abs(randn()) > 1.96 ? "jubilant" : "downtrodden"
explanation = mymood == "jubilant" ? "" : "failed to"
println("Just so you know, so-and-so is absolutely $(mymood) because their simulation $(explanation) converged.")


Explain why there is an extra space whenever so-and-so’s mood is jubilant.



Functional Version: ifelse()
The performance of code with hot loops (that is, code that is expected to execute thousands of times in a program or script) can be quite sensitive to minor tweaks. One example is the presence of branches. Modern CPUs are equipped with aggressive branch predictors that attempt to mitigate the cost of branching but they have limitations.
In some cases, it may be cheaper to avoid branching altogether by paying the cost of executing both branches. This is precisely the purpose of ifelse() in the Julia language:

x = 0.5 * randn()

# this branches (maybe)
if x < 0
  x^2
else
  sqrt(x)
end


# this does not branch
# both expressions below are evaluated before checking the condition.
ifelse(x < 0, x^2, sqrt(x))


ifelse(true, 0, error("stop execution!"))







Noteifelse() in other languages



In the Python and R languages, the ifelse() function is primarily used to vectorize conditional statements. Julia’s version also supports vectorization, e.g. ifelse.(condition, x, y).

title: Control Flow
text:
Repeated Evaluation

for Loop

for i in 1:10
  println(i)
end

Just like condtional statements, loops can be nested.

for i in 1:10
  for j in 1:5
    println(i * j)
  end
end

Julia supports nesting within a single line:

for i in 1:10, j in 1:5
  println(i * j)
end



while Loop

while condition1
  # do something
end



Loop Overrides
You can break out of innermost loop.

for i in 1:10
  # do something
  if condition1
    break # skip remaining loop
  end
end

You can also continue to skip over a particular iteration.

for i in 1:10
  # do something
  if condition1
    continue # skip to next iteration
  end
  # do something
end



Example: Displaying a Tic-Tac-Toe board
A Tic-Tac-Toe board consists of 9 spaces arranged in a 3 by 3 grid. If we include characters to represent the grid, then we need 5 characters per row for a total of 25 characters. Let’s display an empty board:

for i in 1:5
  row_i = ""
  if iszero(i % 2)
    row_i *= "─┼─┼─"
  else
    for j in 1:5
      row_i *= ifelse(iszero(j % 2), "│", " ")
    end
  end
  println(row_i)
end



Compatibility with Iterators
Loops in Julia are compatible with any iterable object. For example, the built-in collections in Julia implement the iteration interface.

x = [10, 20, 30]

for item in x
  println(item)
end


for (i, item) in enumerate(x)
  println("index: ", i, ", value: ", item)
end


for item in reverse(x)
  println(item)
end


d = Dict("Alice" => 4, "Bob" => 2)
for (key, val) in d
  println("They key $(key) maps to value $(val)")
end







TipLaziness is a virtue



The reverse() function above does not sort() the array x! Instead, it exploits the structure of the underlying data type to reverse the iteration. This avoids memory allocation and extra computation.








TipIteration Style



The proper style for iterating over an Array is to use eachindex() or axes(). The reason is that, while Julia uses 1-based indexing, it supports arbitrary indexing styles.

title: Control Flow
text:
Error Handling
Julia provides several built-in exception types to handle errors or otherwise halt execution and display an informative message.

1 / 0     # division expanding to floating point
div(1, 0) # Euclidean division (integers only)


error("Eternity lies ahead of us, and behind. Have you drunk your fill?")

In many cases, it is enough to use an assertion with @assert.

x = -1
@assert x >= 0
sqrt(x)

title: QR Decomposition
text:
Given \(\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\), QR decomposition factorizes \(\mathbf{A}\) as \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R}\).

Usually use economy QR, \(\mathbf{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}\) where \(r\) is numerical rank.
\(\mathbf{Q}\) has orthonormal columns; i.e. \(\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}\) (identity matrix).
\(\mathbf{R}\) has upper triangular structure (but not square in general).
Complexity: \(2np^{2} - \frac{2}{3} p^{3}\) flops; \(\mathbf{Q}\) is not stored and requires additional \(2np^{2} - \frac{2}{3} p^{3}\) flops (Householder method)
Less numerically stable compared to other methods for linear systems.



Input: Vectors \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
Output: The Gram-Schmidt algorithm generates a sequence of orthonormal vectors \(\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots\).

For \(i=1,\ldots,k\):

Orthogonalization: \(\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{a}_i - [(\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1}]\).
Test for linear independence: if \(\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{0}\), quit.
Normalization: \(\mathbf{q}_i = \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i / \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|\).

If G-S does not stop early (in step 2), \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_k\) are linearly independent.
If G-S stops early in iteration \(i=j\), then \(\mathbf{a}_j\) is a linear combination of \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}\) and \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}\) are linearly independent.



Code
# Inputs
a1 = [0.5, 2]
a2 = [1.5, 0.5]

p1 = plot([0 0; a1[1] a2[1]], [0 0; a1[2] a2[2]],
  arrow = true, color = :purple, axis = ([], false), legend = :none,
  xlims = (-2, 2), ylims = (-2, 2),
  annotations = [
    (a1[1] + 0.2, a1[2], L"a_1"),
    (a2[1] + 0.2, a2[2], L"a_2")
  ],
  framestyle = :origin,
  aspect_ratio = :equal,
  title = "1"
)
t = 0:0.01:2π
plot!(p1, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray)

# orthogonalizing a1
q̃1 = copy(a1) 
p2 = plot([0 0; q̃1[1] a2[1]], [0 0; q̃1[2] a2[2]],
  arrow = true, color = [:red :purple], axis = ([], false), legend = :none,
  xlims = (-2, 2), ylims = (-2, 2),
  annotations = [
    (q̃1[1] + 0.2, q̃1[2], L"\tilde{q}_1"),
    (a2[1] + 0.2, a2[2], L"a_2")
  ],
  framestyle = :origin,
  aspect_ratio = :equal,
  title = "2"
)
t = 0:0.01:2π
plot!(p2, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray)

# normalizing q̃1
q1 = q̃1 / norm(q̃1) 
p3 = plot([0 0; q1[1] a2[1]], [0 0; q1[2] a2[2]],
  arrow = true, color = [:green :purple],
  axis = ([], false), legend = :none,
  xlims = (-2, 2), ylims = (-2, 2),
  annotations = [
    (q1[1] + 0.2, q1[2], L"q_1"),
    (a2[1] + 0.2, a2[2], L"a_2")
  ],
  framestyle = :origin,
  aspect_ratio = :equal,
  title = "3"
)
t = 0:0.01:2π
plot!(p3, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray)

# orthogonalizing a2
q̃2 = a2 - dot(a2, q1) * q1
p4 = plot([0 0 0; q1[1] a2[1] q̃2[1]], [0 0 0; q1[2] a2[2] q̃2[2]], 
  arrow = true, color = [:green :purple :red], axis = ([], false), legend = :none,
  xlims = (-1.5, 1.5), ylims = (-1.5, 1.5),
  annotations = [
    (q1[1] + 0.2, q1[2], L"q_1"),
    (a2[1] + 0.2, a2[2], L"a_2"),
    (q̃2[1] + 0.2, q̃2[2] - 0.2, L"\tilde{q}_2"),
    ((a2[1] + q̃2[1]) / 2 + 1.2, (a2[2] + q̃2[2]) / 2, L"-(q_1' a_2)q_1")
  ],
  framestyle = :origin,
  aspect_ratio = :equal,
  title = "4"
)
t = 0:0.01:2π
plot!(p4, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray)
plot!(p4, [a2[1]; q̃2[1]], [a2[2]; q̃2[2]], arrow = true, color = :black)

# normalizing q̃2
q2 = q̃2 / norm(q̃2) 
p5 = plot([0 0; q1[1] q2[1]], [0 0; q1[2] q2[2]],
  arrow = true, color = :green,
  axis = ([], false), legend = :none,
  xlims = (-1.5, 1.5), ylims = (-1.5, 1.5),
  annotations = [
    (q1[1] + 0.3, q1[2] + 0.1, L"q_1"),
    (q2[1] + 0.3, q2[2], L"q_2")
  ],
  framestyle = :origin,
  aspect_ratio = :equal,
  title = "5"
)
t = 0:0.01:2π
plot!(p5, sin.(t), cos.(t), color = :gray)

plot(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5)








Note



All circles shown here are unit circles with radius 1. The first three circles appear smaller to work around a “clipping” issue in the plotting engine.



# n = 5, k = 3
@show a1 = randn(5)
@show a2 = randn(5)
@show a3 = randn(5);


# for i = 1
# orthogonalization
@show q̃1 = copy(a1)
# test for linear independence
@show norm(q̃1) ≈ 0
# normalization
@show q1 = q̃1 / norm(q̃1);


# for i = 2
# orthogonalization
@show q̃2 = a2 - (q1'a2) * q1
# test for linear independence
@show norm(q̃2) ≈ 0
# normalization
@show q2 = q̃2 / norm(q̃2);


# for i = 3
# orthogonalization
@show q̃3 = a3 - (q1'a3) * q1 - (q2'a3) * q2
# test for linear independence
@show norm(q̃3) ≈ 0
# Normalization
@show q3 = q̃3 / norm(q̃3);


# test for orthonormality of q1, q2, q3
@show norm(q1), norm(q2), norm(q3)
@show q1'q2
@show q1'q3
@show q2'q3;




Computational complexity of G-S algorithm:

Step 1 of iteration \(i\) requires (1) \(i-1\) inner products, \(\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i\), which costs \((i-1)(2n-1)\) flops, and (2) \(2n(i-1)\) flops to compute \(\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\).
Step 2 of iteration \(i\) requires less than \(n\) flops.
Step 3 of iteration \(i\) requires \(3n\) flops to normalize \(\|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|\).
Assuming no early termination, total computational cost of the GS algorithm to orthonormalize a set of \(k\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is: \[
\sum_{i=1}^k [(4n-1) (i - 1) + 3n] = (4n - 1) \frac{k(k-1)}{2} + 3nk \approx 2nk^2 = O(nk^2),
\]

using \(\sum_{i=1}^k (i - 1) = k(k-1)/2\).



The operations in GS can be compactly expressed as
\[
\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R},
\]
where \(\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{a}_1 \, \cdots \, \mathbf{a}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\), \(\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{q}_1 \, \cdots \, \mathbf{q}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) satisfying \(\mathbf{Q}'\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}_k\) (\(\mathbf{Q}\) has orthonormal columns), and \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) is an upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal elements.
What are the entries in \(\mathbf{R}\)? In the \(i\)-th iteration of the Gram-Schmidt algorithm
\[\begin{eqnarray*}
\text{Orthogonalization step: } & & \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{a}_i - (\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 - \cdots - (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1} \\
\text{Normalization step: } & & \mathbf{q}_i = \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i / \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|.
\end{eqnarray*}\]
Therefore, \[
\mathbf{a}_i =  (\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1} + \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\| \mathbf{q}_i.
\]
This tells us \(R_{ij} = \mathbf{q}_i' \mathbf{a}_j\) for \(i < j\) and \(R_{ii} = \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|\).
Thus overall Gram-Schmidt algorithm performs \[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | & | \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{a}_k \\ | & | & & | & | \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | & | \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_k \\ | & | & & | & | \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
\|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_1\| & \mathbf{q}_1'\mathbf{a}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_{k-1}  & \mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_k \\
& \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_2\| & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_2' \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_2' \mathbf{a}_k \\
& & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
& & & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_{k-1}\| & \mathbf{q}_{k-1}' \mathbf{a}_k \\
& & & & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_k\|
\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R}.
\]






Warning



The Gram-Schmidt algorithm is numerically unstable. The specific issue that arises is that the basis vectors \(\mathbf{q}_{k}\) may lose their orthogonality. The modified Gram-Schmidt is preferred. In your homework you will implement QR via Householder reflections, which is more stable and efficient (the basis vectors are computed implicitly).





Now look at solving linear systems (full column rank), assuming we already have \(\mathbf{Q}\) and \(\mathbf{R}\):
\[
\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \equiv \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b} \implies \text{Solve}~\mathbf{R} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{y}
\]

Form RHS: \(2np\) flops (since \(\mathbf{Q}\) is \(n \times p\))
Solve with backward substitution: \(p^{2}\) flops
Total: \(2np + p^{2}\)




Least squares problem \(\min_{\beta}~\frac{1}{2} \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X}\beta\|_{2}^{2}\) has the same complexity:

Why? Use properties of orthonormal matrices…
Reduction to \(\min_{\beta}~\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{Q}^\top \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{R}\beta\|_{2}^{2}\).
Fit \(\beta\) (QR + solve): \(2(n-1)p^{2} - \frac{2}{3} p^{3} + 2np\)
Standard errors for estimates: Requires inverting \(\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}\) (one of a few cases where it is acceptable!)

We can be far more clever about inverting the matrix. View the problem of computing \((\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}\) as:
\[
\text{Solve}~\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X} \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I} \quad \equiv \quad \mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{R} \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{I};
\]
that is, we solve two triangular systems for the matrix-valued variable \(\mathbf{\Sigma}\).






Note



Note that \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta})\) depends on \(\mathbf{X}\) in linear regression, but the explicit form for the standard errors depends on whatever assumptions we are willing to make about the random component (e.g. normal errors).

X = [ones(length(y)) Matrix(select(longley, Not(:Employed)))]

Solve for coefficients:

qrX = qr(X)
β = qrX \ y

Get standard errors:

r = y - X*β # residuals
s² = r'r / (length(y) - length(β)) # correction: n - p
tmp = UpperTriangular(qrX.R)' \ (1.0 * I(length(β))) # trisolve 1
Σβ = UpperTriangular(qrX.R) \ tmp # trisolve 2
sqrt.(s² * diag(Σβ)) # variances on diagonal

Back in R:

fit.longley <- lm(Employed ~ . + 1, data = $longley)


# Fitted β
coef(fit.longley)


# Can see standard errors here
print(coef(summary(fit.longley)));

title: QR Decomposition
text:
Input: Vectors \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
Output: The Gram-Schmidt algorithm generates a sequence of orthonormal vectors \(\mathbf{q}_1, \mathbf{q}_2, \ldots\).

For \(i=1,\ldots,k\):

Orthogonalization: \(\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{a}_i - [(\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1}]\).
Test for linear independence: if \(\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{0}\), quit.
Normalization: \(\mathbf{q}_i = \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i / \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|\).

If G-S does not stop early (in step 2), \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_k\) are linearly independent.
If G-S stops early in iteration \(i=j\), then \(\mathbf{a}_j\) is a linear combination of \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}\) and \(\mathbf{a}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_{j-1}\) are linearly independent.

a2 = [1.5, 0.5]

title: QR Decomposition
text:
Computational complexity of G-S algorithm:

Step 1 of iteration \(i\) requires (1) \(i-1\) inner products, \(\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i, \ldots, \mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i\), which costs \((i-1)(2n-1)\) flops, and (2) \(2n(i-1)\) flops to compute \(\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\).
Step 2 of iteration \(i\) requires less than \(n\) flops.
Step 3 of iteration \(i\) requires \(3n\) flops to normalize \(\|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|\).
Assuming no early termination, total computational cost of the GS algorithm to orthonormalize a set of \(k\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is: \[
\sum_{i=1}^k [(4n-1) (i - 1) + 3n] = (4n - 1) \frac{k(k-1)}{2} + 3nk \approx 2nk^2 = O(nk^2),
\]

using \(\sum_{i=1}^k (i - 1) = k(k-1)/2\).

title: QR Decomposition
text:
The operations in GS can be compactly expressed as
\[
\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R},
\]
where \(\mathbf{A} = (\mathbf{a}_1 \, \cdots \, \mathbf{a}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\), \(\mathbf{Q} = (\mathbf{q}_1 \, \cdots \, \mathbf{q}_k) \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k}\) satisfying \(\mathbf{Q}'\mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{I}_k\) (\(\mathbf{Q}\) has orthonormal columns), and \(\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}\) is an upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal elements.
What are the entries in \(\mathbf{R}\)? In the \(i\)-th iteration of the Gram-Schmidt algorithm
\[\begin{eqnarray*}
\text{Orthogonalization step: } & & \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i = \mathbf{a}_i - (\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 - \cdots - (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1} \\
\text{Normalization step: } & & \mathbf{q}_i = \tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i / \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|.
\end{eqnarray*}\]
Therefore, \[
\mathbf{a}_i =  (\mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_1 + \cdots + (\mathbf{q}_{i-1}' \mathbf{a}_i) \mathbf{q}_{i-1} + \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\| \mathbf{q}_i.
\]
This tells us \(R_{ij} = \mathbf{q}_i' \mathbf{a}_j\) for \(i < j\) and \(R_{ii} = \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_i\|\).
Thus overall Gram-Schmidt algorithm performs \[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | & | \\ \mathbf{a}_1 & \mathbf{a}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{a}_k \\ | & | & & | & | \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} | & | & & | & | \\ \mathbf{q}_1 & \mathbf{q}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_k \\ | & | & & | & | \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}
\|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_1\| & \mathbf{q}_1'\mathbf{a}_2 & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_{k-1}  & \mathbf{q}_1' \mathbf{a}_k \\
& \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_2\| & \cdots & \mathbf{q}_2' \mathbf{a}_{k-1} & \mathbf{q}_2' \mathbf{a}_k \\
& & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
& & & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_{k-1}\| & \mathbf{q}_{k-1}' \mathbf{a}_k \\
& & & & \|\tilde{\mathbf{q}}_k\|
\end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{R}.
\]






Warning



The Gram-Schmidt algorithm is numerically unstable. The specific issue that arises is that the basis vectors \(\mathbf{q}_{k}\) may lose their orthogonality. The modified Gram-Schmidt is preferred. In your homework you will implement QR via Householder reflections, which is more stable and efficient (the basis vectors are computed implicitly).

title: Iterative Methods
text:
Background: Graph Theory
A graph is a mathematical abstraction for networks, which in turn model certain kinds of relations in applications (of graph theory). A graph is defined by

a set of vertices \(V\) (or nodes or points or actors…), and
a set of edges \(E = \{(x,y) : x,y \in V\}\) (or links or arcs or…).

Graphs can be directed or undirected, depending on whether the underlying relation is asymmetric or symmetric, respectively. As such, a graph can be specified using a (weighted) adjacency matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) with entries
\[
a_{ij} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if $(i,j) \in E$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}.
\]
Various important quantities can be derived from \(\mathbf{A}\)

Out Degree: \(d_{i}^{+} = \sum_{j} a_{ij} = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{1}\) (if we treat rows of \(\mathbf{A}\) as the originating nodes)
In Degree: \(d_{i}^{-} = \sum_{j} a_{ji} = \mathbf{1}^{\top} \mathbf{A}\)
If \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric, the graph is directed and so we only speak of the degree \(d_{i} = d_{i}^{+} = d_{i}^{-}\).

Spectral graph theory relates eigenvalues/eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{A}\) or its Laplacian to properties of graphs, and has important applications to high dimensional statistics and machine learning.

title: Iterative Methods
text:
The Problem





Larry Page imagines a random surfer wandering on internet according to following rules:

From a page \(i\) with \(r_i>0\)

with probability \(p\), they randomly choose a link on page \(i\) (uniformly) and follows that link to the next page

with probability \(1-p\), they randomly choose one page from the set of all \(n\) pages (uniformly) and proceeds to that page

From a page \(i\) with \(r_i=0\) (a dangling page), they randomly choose one page from the set of all \(n\) pages (uniformly) and proceeds to that page

Here \(r_i\) is the out-degree of page \(i\) and \(\mathbf{A}  \in \{0,1\}^{n \times n}\) the connectivity matrix of webpages with entries \[
a_{ij} = \begin{cases}
1 &  \text{if page $i$ links to page $j$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}.
\]

\(n \approx 10^9\) in May 2017.

The description above defines a Markov chain on the space of \(n\) pages. Markov chain theory tells us that the stationary distribution of this Markov chain gives the ranks (probabilities) of each page.

A vector \(\mathbf{x}\) is a stationary distribution if it is a top left eigenvector of the transition matrix \(\mathbf{P}\) corresponding to eigenvalue 1.- Equivalently it can be cast as the solution to the linear equation \[
(\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{P}^T) \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}.
\]
GE/LU will take \(2 \times (10^9)^3/3/10^{12} \approx 6.66 \times 10^{14}\) seconds \(\approx 20\) million years on a tera-flop supercomputer!
Numerical analyst Gene Golub called this the largest matrix computation in world.
Iterative methods come to the rescue.

title: Iterative Methods
text:
Jacobi Method
\[
x_i^{(k+1)} = \frac{b_i - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} a_{ij} x_j^{(k)} - \sum_{j=i+1}^n a_{ij} x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.
\]
Rewrite using splitting \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L} + \mathbf{D} + \mathbf{U}\) \[
\mathbf{D} \mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = - (\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{U}) \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{b},
\]
resulting in the iteration map (algorithm)
\[
\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = - \mathbf{D}^{-1} (\mathbf{L} + \mathbf{U}) \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{D}^{-1} \mathbf{b} = - \mathbf{D}^{-1} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{D}^{-1} \mathbf{b}.
\]

Convergence for diagonally dominant \(\mathbf{A}\).
One round costs \(2n^2\) flops with an unstructured \(\mathbf{A}\).
Gain over GE/LU if it converges in \(O(n)\) iterations.
Huge savings for sparse or structured \(\mathbf{A}\). By structured, we mean the matrix-vector multiplication \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{v}\) is fast (\(O(n)\) or \(O(n \log n)\)).

title: Iterative Methods
text:
Gauss-Seidel
\[
x_i^{(k+1)} = \frac{b_i - \sum_{j=1}^{i-1} a_{ij} x_j^{(k+1)} - \sum_{j=i+1}^n a_{ij} x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.
\]
Rewrite with splitting \((\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{L}) \mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = - \mathbf{U} \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + \mathbf{b}\), that is, \[
\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)} = - (\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{L})^{-1} \mathbf{U} \mathbf{x}^{(k)} + (\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{L})^{-1} \mathbf{b}.
\]

Converges for any \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\) for symmetric and positive definite \(\mathbf{A}\).
Convergence rate of Gauss-Seidel is the spectral radius of the \((\mathbf{D} + \mathbf{L})^{-1} \mathbf{U}\).

title: Iterative Methods
text:
Conjugate Gradients

Invented by Magnus Hestenes and Eduard Stiefel in 60s. See @hestenes1952methods for details.
Idea: Solving \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) is equivalent to minimizing the quadratic function \(\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{x}^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{x}\).
Consider a simple idea: coordinate descent, that is to update components \(x_j\) alternatingly. Same as the Gauss-Seidel iteration. Usually it takes too many iterations.

Kershaw’s results for a laser fusion problem.



Method
Number of Iterations




Gauss-Seidel
208,000


Block SOR methods
765


Incomplete Cholesky conjugate gradient
25



Message: Conjugate gradients and its variants are the top-notch iterative methods for solving huge, structured linear systems.





How can we avoid the issue in the picture?

Define the residual \(\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} =: \mathbf{r}(\mathbf{x})\)
A set of vectors \(\{\mathbf{p}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{p}^{(t)}\}\) are said to be conjugate with respect to \(\mathbf{A}\) if \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \mathbf{p}_i^T \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}_j = 0, \quad \text{for all } i \ne j.
\end{eqnarray*}
\]
For example, eigen-vectors of \(\mathbf{A}\) are conjugate to each other. Why?

Conjugate Direction Method: Given a set of conjugate vectors \(\{\mathbf{p}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{p}^{(n-1)}\}\), at iteration \(t\), we search along the conjugate direction \(\mathbf{p}^{(t)}\) \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} = \mathbf{x}^{(t)} + \alpha^{(t)} \mathbf{p}^{(t)},
\end{eqnarray*}
\] where \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \alpha^{(t)} = - \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(t)T} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(t)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}
\end{eqnarray*}
\] is the optimal step length.

Theorem: In conjugate direction method, \(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\) converges to the solution in at most \(n\) steps.
Intuition: Look at a graph.






Conjugate Gradient Method: generate \(\mathbf{p}^{(t)}\) using only \(\mathbf{p}^{(t-1)}\) \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \mathbf{p}^{(t)} = - \mathbf{r}^{(t)} + \beta^{(t)} \mathbf{p}^{(t-1)},
\end{eqnarray*}
\] where \(\beta^{(t)}\) is determined by the conjugacy condition \(\mathbf{p}^{(t-1)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)} = 0\) \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \beta^{(t)} = \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(t)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t-1)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(t-1)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t-1)}}.
\end{eqnarray*}
\]

Algorithm (preliminary version)
Given \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\), \(\mathbf{A}\), and \(\mathbf{b}\).

Initialize: \(\mathbf{r}^{(0)} \gets \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}^{(0)} - \mathbf{b}\), \(\mathbf{p}^{(0)} \gets - \mathbf{r}^{(0)}\), \(t=0\)
While \(\mathbf{r}^{(t)} \ne \mathbf{0}\)

\(\alpha^{(t)} \gets - \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(t)T} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(t)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}\)
\(\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} \gets \mathbf{x}^{(t)} + \alpha^{(t)} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\)
\(\mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} \gets \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} - \mathbf{b}\)
\(\beta^{(t+1)} \gets \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(t+1)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(t)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}\)
\(\mathbf{p}^{(t+1)} \gets - \mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} + \beta^{(t+1)} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\)
\(t \gets t+1\)


The initial conjugate direction \(\mathbf{p}^{(0)} \gets - \mathbf{r}^{(0)}\) is crucial.


Algorithm (economical version)
Saves one matrix-vector multiplication.
Given \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\), \(\mathbf{A}\), and \(\mathbf{b}\).

Initialize: \(\mathbf{r}^{(0)} \gets \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}^{(0)} - \mathbf{b}\), \(\mathbf{p}^{(0)} \gets - \mathbf{r}^{(0)}\), \(t=0\)
While \(\mathbf{r}^{(t)} \ne \mathbf{0}\)
\(\alpha^{(t)} \gets \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(t)T} \mathbf{r}^{(t)}}{\mathbf{p}^{(t)T} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}}\)
\(\mathbf{x}^{(t+1)} \gets \mathbf{x}^{(t)} + \alpha^{(t)} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\)
\(\mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} \gets \mathbf{r}^{(t)} + \alpha^{(t)} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\)
\(\beta^{(t+1)} \gets \frac{\mathbf{r}^{(t+1)T} \mathbf{r}^{(t+1)}}{\mathbf{r}^{(t)T} \mathbf{r}^{(t)}}\)
\(\mathbf{p}^{(t+1)} \gets - \mathbf{r}^{(t+1)} + \beta^{(t+1)} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\)
\(t \gets t+1\)


Computation cost per iteration is one matrix vector multiplication: \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\).

Consider the PageRank problem: \(\mathbf{A}\) has dimension \(n \approx 10^{9}\) but is highly structured (sparse + low rank). Each matrix vector multiplication should only take about \(O(n)\) flops.



Theory

\(\mathbf{r}^{(t)}\) are mutually orthogonal.
\(\{\mathbf{r}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{r}^{(t)}\}\) is contained in the Krylov subspace of degree \(t\) for \(\mathbf{r}^{(0)}\), denoted by \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\cal K}(\mathbf{r}^{(0)}; t) = \text{span} \{\mathbf{r}^{(0)},\mathbf{A} \mathbf{r}^{(0)}, \mathbf{A}^2 \mathbf{r}^{(0)}, \ldots, \mathbf{A}^{t} \mathbf{r}^{(0)}\}.
\end{eqnarray*}
\]
\(\{\mathbf{p}^{(0)},\ldots,\mathbf{p}^{(t)}\}\) is contained in \({\cal K}(\mathbf{r}^{(0)}; t)\).
\(\mathbf{p}^{(0)}, \ldots, \mathbf{p}^{(t)}\) are conjugate with respect to \(\mathbf{A}\).


The iterates \(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\) converge to the solution in at most \(n\) steps.
Theorem: If \(\mathbf{A}\) has \(r\) distinct eigenvalues, \(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\) converges to solution \(\mathbf{x}^*\) in at most \(r\) steps.

title: Iterative Methods
text:
Other Krylov subspace methods
The CG method is for solving \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\), with \(\mathbf{A}\) positive definite (minimizing a quadratic). A variety of other modern iterative methods use the same machinery of CG and extend its reach to different problems.

MINRES (minimum residual method): symmetric indefinite \(\mathbf{A}\).
Bi-CG (bi-conjugate gradient): unsymmetric \(\mathbf{A}\).
Bi-CGSTAB (Bi-CG stabilized): improved version of Bi-CG.
GMRES (generalized minimum residual method): current de facto method for unsymmetric \(\mathbf{A}\). E.g., PageRank problem.
Lanczos method: top eigen-pairs of a large symmetric matrix.
Arnoldi method: top eigen-pairs of a large unsymmetric matrix.
Lanczos bidiagonalization algorithm: top singular triplets of large matrix.
LSQR: least square problem \(\min \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X} \beta\|_2^2\). Algebraically equivalent to applying CG to the normal equation \((\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \lambda^2 I) \beta = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\).
LSMR: least square problem \(\min \|\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{X} \beta\|_2^2\). Algebraically equivalent to applying MINRES to the normal equation \((\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{X} + \lambda^2 I) \beta = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{y}\).

title: LU Decomposition
text:
LU decomposition is effectively Gaussian Elimination; it records the operations and the result of such operations into two triangular matrices, \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L}\mathbf{U}\). - Uncommon in statistics because most of time statisticians deal with positive (semi)definite matrices. - Applies generally to arbitrary matrices, though factors are only “almost” triangular.






Note




History: Chinese mathematical text The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, Issac Newton and Carl Friedrich Gauss.
A toy example illustrating GE.





An elementary operator matrix is the identity matrix with the 0 in position \((j,k)\) replaced by \(c\) \[
    \mathbf{E}_{jk}(c) = \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & & \\
    & \ddots & \\
    & & 1 & \\
    & & & \ddots & \\
    & & c & & 1 & \\
    & & & & & \ddots \\
    & & & & & & 1
    \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{I} + c \mathbf{e}_j \mathbf{e}_k^T.
\]






Note



Closely related to Householder transformation. Reminder that here \(\mathbf{e}_{j}\) is the \(j\)-th standard basis vector in \(\mathbf{R}^{d}\), which has all 0s except in the \(j\)-th place.


Each \(\mathbf{E}_{jk}(c)\) is unit triangular, full rank, and its inverse is
\[
\mathbf{E}_{jk}^{-1}(c) = \mathbf{E}_{jk}(-c).
\]
\(\mathbf{E}_{jk}(c)\) left-multiplies an \(n \times m\) matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) effectively replace its \(j\)-th row \(\mathbf{x}_{j\cdot}\) by \(c \mathbf{x}_{k \cdot} + \mathbf{x}_{j \cdot}\)
\[
    \mathbf{E}_{jk}(c) \times \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{E}_{jk}(c) \times \begin{pmatrix}
    & & \\
    \cdots & \mathbf{x}_{k\cdot} & \cdots \\
    & & \\
    \cdots & \mathbf{x}_{j\cdot} & \cdots \\
    & &
    \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
    & & \\
    \cdots & \mathbf{x}_{k\cdot} & \cdots \\
    & & \\
    \cdots & c \mathbf{x}_{k\cdot} + \mathbf{x}_{j\cdot} & \cdots \\
    & &
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]






Note



All for the low cost of \(2m\) flops.


Gaussian elimination applies a sequence of elementary operator matrices to transform the linear system \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) to an upper triangular system
\[\begin{eqnarray*}
    \mathbf{E}_{n,n-1}(c_{n,n-1}) \cdots \mathbf{E}_{21}(c_{21}) \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} &=& \mathbf{E}_{n,n-1}(c_{n,n-1}) \cdots \mathbf{E}_{21}(c_{21}) \mathbf{b} \\
    \mathbf{U} \mathbf{x} &=& \mathbf{b}_{\text{new}}.
\end{eqnarray*}\]



For the first column, we apply several elementary operator matrices on the left: \[
    \mathbf{M}_1 = \mathbf{E}_{n1}(c_{n1}) \cdots \mathbf{E}_{31}(c_{31}) \mathbf{E}_{21}(c_{21}) = \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & \\
    c_{21} & \\
    & \ddots & \\
    c_{n1} & & 1
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
For the \(k\)-th column, we do the same: \[
    \mathbf{M}_k = \mathbf{E}_{nk}(c_{nk}) \cdots \mathbf{E}_{k+1,k}(c_{k+1,k}) = \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & \\
    & \ddots \\
    & & 1 & \\
    & & c_{k+1,k} & 1\\
    & & \vdots & & \ddots \\
    & &  c_{n,k} & & & 1
    \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The \(\mathbf{M}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{M}_{n-1}\) matrices are called Gauss transformations. Gaussian elimination does \[
\mathbf{M}_{n-1} \cdots \mathbf{M}_1 \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U}.
\]
Let \[\begin{equation*}
\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{M}_1^{-1} \cdots \mathbf{M}_{n-1}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}  
    1 & & & & \\
    \,- c_{21} & \ddots & & & \\
    & & 1 & & \\
    \, - c_{k+1,1} & & - c_{k+1,k} & & \\
    & & \vdots & & \ddots \\
    \,- c_{n1} & & - c_{nk} & & & 1
    \end{pmatrix}.
\end{equation*}\] Thus we have the LU decomposition \[
\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{U},
\]
where \(\mathbf{L}\) is unit lower triangular and \(\mathbf{U}\) is upper triangular.









The total cost to compute factors is \(\frac{2}{3} n^{3}\) flops for square systems.
Solving with LU is the cost of two triangular solves: \(2n^{2}\).





Solve \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}\), or \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}_{i} = \mathbf{e}_{i}\).
Exploiting 0s in RHS reduces complexity of each solve, changing cost of triangular solves from \(2n^{3} to \frac{4}{3}n^{3}\).
Cost to inverest with Gaussian elimination: \(2n^{3}\) flops, which is 3 times more expensive than just solving with LU!







Note



Reasons to invert a matrix:

Need standard errors.
Number of RHSs is much greater than \(n\) (multivariate regression)
\(n\) is small, and you use StaticArrays.jl to do so blazingly fast.

title: Eigen Decomposition
text:
Eigenvalue decomposition
Some facts and definitions:

Eigenvalues are defined as roots of the characteristic equation \(\det(\lambda \mathbf{I}_n - \mathbf{A})=0\).
If \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(\mathbf{A}\), then there exist non-zero \(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(\mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}^T \mathbf{A} = \lambda \mathbf{y}^T\). The \(\mathbf{x}\) and \(\mathbf{y}\) are called the (column) eigenvector and row eigenvector of \(\mathbf{A}\) associated with the eigenvalue \(\lambda\).
\(\mathbf{A}\) is singular if and only if it has at least one 0 eigenvalue.
Eigenvectors associated with distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
Eigenvalues of an upper or lower triangular matrix are its diagonal entries: \(\lambda_i = a_{ii}\).
Eigenvalues of an idempotent matrix are either 0 or 1.
Eigenvalues of an orthogonal matrix have complex modulus 1.
In most statistical applications, we deal with eigenvalues/eigenvectors of symmetric matrices. The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a real symmetric matrix are real.
Eigenvectors associated with distinct eigenvalues of a symmetry matrix are orthogonal.

Eigen-decompostion of a symmetric matrix: \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U} \Lambda \mathbf{U}^T\), where

\(\Lambda = \text{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\)
columns of \(\mathbf{U}\) are the eigenvectors, which are (or can be chosen to be) mutually orthonormal. Thus \(\mathbf{U}\) is an orthogonal matrix.

title: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
A (column) vector \(\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\):
\[
\mathbf{x} = \begin{pmatrix}
x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_n
\end{pmatrix} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n).
\]

\(n\) is the dimension (or length or size) of the vector.
\(x_i\) is the \(i\)-th entry (or element or component or coefficient) of \(\mathbf{x}\).
A vector of length \(n\) is called an \(n\)-vector.

A row vector \(\mathbf{x}^{\top} = (x_1 \, x_2 \, \ldots x_n)\) (without commas).

JuliaR



# a (column) vector in Julia
x = [1, -1, 2, 0, 3]

Julia uses square brackets [] to define vectors. The data type is inferred from the elements supplied. The example here defines a Vector{Int}, a vector with integer types.

x'

We will be working over the real number \(\mathbb{R}\), so the two will be equivalent for our purposes.



R"""
x <- $x # pull data from Julia side
