title: The Unix Shell
text:
Goals

Develop a sense of how to navigate on a Linux based system using cd, pwd, and ls.
Practice using a command-line interface.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
What is Unix?
UNIX is a broad term for a collection of operating systems that no longer exist. These systems emerged in the late 1960s/1970s when time-sharing was an important computing model. Its various projects represent tight collaboration between academic circles and industrial research groups (e.g. Bell Labs).
Although extinct, UNIX spawned descendant UNIX-like, or Linux-like, systems and continues to influence computing to this day. Part of its lasting impact is, arguably, due to the so-called UNIX Philosophy

Write programs that do one thing and do it well.
Write programs to work together.
Write programs to handle text streams, because that is a universal interface.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
What is a Shell?
In the last several decades, humans have interacted with computers in a variety of ways. You are likely reading this on a graphical user interface (GUI). While appealing and (usually) intuitive, GUIs do not scale well to certain tasks. A command-line interace (CLI) is often an efficient interaction mode for manipulating files on computers and automating various repetitive tasks. Both GUIs and CLIs are examples of shells: they are user interfaces that allow an entity to interact with an OS.
In this class, we will use shell as a shorthand for CLI shell, which operate through text-based inputs and outputs. The class Docker image has three shells:

zsh: Z shell, which is the default. This default is used by modern MacOS, too. It is a good option for interactive work.
bash: Bourne Again Shell. It is a good option for scripting because it respects portability and adheres to well-established standards.
sh: Bourne Shell. This is the standard for system-level work and operations, and will not be relevant to us.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
But… why?
While CLIs have a learning curve that involve learning various commands, they also:

allow simple operations to be combined, forming new, useful programs,
allow commands to be recorded for documentaion, reuse, modification, and automation,
allow programs to be parameterized, extending their use, and
empower the user to be thoughtful, independent, competent, and fast.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
Getting started
The class Docker image creates a container that, by default, will log you in to an interactive shell zsh. You will be greeted by a prompt:
student@STAT206 ~ $
The prompt is fully customizable, but this was chosen to present some information to students in the class:

student: This is the user account you are logged in as when you run a container with our image.
@STAT206: A visual cue that you are in the container, not your own operating system’s environment.
~: The current directory. It is shorthand for your home directory, /home/student. The display will change as you navigate to different locations.
$: A visual cue that you may enter a command.

This brings up two important concepts to keep in mind (regardless of what computer/OS you use):

Everything you do on a computer, you do as a particular user. Users have different permissions that limit or enable access to resources on a computer.
Every command you type into your shell operates within some context, namely the directory you are currently in.







WarningNever use sudo unless it is absolutely necessary



In the past, many programmers would scour StackOverflow and similar websites to figure how to do something on their favorite Linux distro. There is a long tradition of trolling inexperienced users and plenty of misinformation.
Today, a Chat Bot may tell you to use sudo to implement a task you’re struggling to figure out.
Regardless of the source, it has been my experience (and the advice of countless experts) that sudo is almost never needed. Everything in this course has been set up so that you do not need to use it. Avoid running sudo commands on your computer unless you’re willing to accept the consequences.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
Navigating
Upon landing in the container, you will start in /home/student/. You can always check where you are using the print working directory command
pwd

/home/student/

For that matter, you can also check who you are
whoami

student

and list everything around
ls



Some paths may be hidden to you. Use an option to make all visible to you:
ls -a

. .. .bashrc .cache .config .julia .juliaup .local .mamba .micromamba .profile .zcompdump .zshrc

If you spot something interesting, take a look
ls .local

bin lib share

and change directory to go there
cd .local/bin
You can always go up a level
cd ..
or return home should you get lost.
cd ~

title: The Unix Shell
text:
Getting Help
If you want to learn more about what a command does or explore the options it has, use --help. For example,
ls --help
displays everything one needs to know about how to use ls. If you find it difficult to read on your screen, pipe the output to less:
ls --help | less
This lets you scroll interactively using u and d. Exit by typing q.






ImportantThere are no manpages



If you’re familiar with Unix-like systems, you might know about the man command to pull up manuals. Unfortunately, the class image does not include any manpages to reduce image size.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
About Our OS
You should become familiar with the OS used by the class Docker image. It is especially important if you use any external resources to troubleshoot or get help. You should not mix advice for Distro A for Distro B.
We are using Debian Bookworm 12 as our Linux distro. The command cat /etc/os-release is a reliable way to discover this information on a Linux distro. Example Output:

VERSION_CODENAME=bookworm
ID=debian
HOME_URL="https://www.debian.org/"

title: Version Control with Git
text: Blischak JD, Davenport ER, Wilson G (2016) A Quick Introduction to Version Control with Git and GitHub. PLoS Comput Biol 12(1): e1004668. doi: 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004668

title: Version Control with Git
text: Blischak JD, Davenport ER, Wilson G (2016) A Quick Introduction to Version Control with Git and GitHub. PLoS Comput Biol 12(1): e1004668. doi: 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1004668

title: Version Control with Git
text:
Goals

Develop an understanding and appreciation of Git and version control.
Understand the difference between a local and remote repository.
Become familiar with basic Git commands and a basic single user workflow.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
What is Version Control?

An article about computational science in a scientific publication is not the scholarship itself, it is merely the advertising of the scholarship. The actual scholarship is the complete software development environment and the complete set of instructions which generated the figures.

— Buckheit and Donoho (1995), summarizing Jon Claerbout’s ideas on reproducible research in computational sciences.
Researchers (Data Scientists, and other professionals) often need to manage a number of documents:

manuscripts/technical reports
notes
data
images
code
scripts

Today, many of those documents live on a computer.

Tracking different versions of a document by hand is tedious and error-prone.
Tracking the history of a changing document is cumbersome.

Version control has its origins in software development and has increasingly been adopted across various disciplines, including data science.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
What is Git?


A tool for distributed version control.
Originally developed by Linus Torvaldis for managing the Linux kernel.
Multiple people own and can edit copies of a repository.
Git operates on changes between versions of a document, effectively tracking line-by-line changes.
Each version of the repository exists as a commit, or snapshot.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
The model
Git keeps track of versions for various files, along with a log that tells us about why things changed.






working directory: the directory on your machine that represents your repository of files under version control.

These are just the files and directories that make up a project. There is no history or version control history.

staging area: files that you tag to commit changes are said to be staged / in the staging area.
local repo: your local repository; the collection of all the files in your folder + changes + history.

This consists only of your commits. Any changes/edits to files not committed are not in the local repository.
Your commits are linked to each other. This lets us go back in time to a different state of the working directory.

remote repo: a foreign version that lives elsewhere; usually a backup on GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
commit: a snapshot of the project. This consists of specific files that were added/removed/edited + an informative message by the commit author.

The main idea is that git helps you put your projects under version control by examining your working tree, comparing to the local repo, and informing you of changes that have occurred. It is then incumbent on YOU to manage those changes and move them onto the staging area to be organized into commits stored in the local repo.






NoteBranches in Git



Git allows you to maintain multiple versions of the same workspace with separate commits using branches. By default, Git initializes your local repository with a main or master branch.
We will revisit branching much later in the course when we start using Git to collaborate with others.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
Basic commands
The list below is by no means exhaustive.

git init
This initializes a working directory as a local Git repository. Specifically, it creates a .git directory to store the history and metadata about various files in the repository.


git add <name of a file or directory>
Adds files to the staging area so that you can create a commit.


git commit
Opens an editor to draft a message associated with your proposed commit. This command supports various additional options.

Add the message in-line: git commit -m "This is my commit message"
Edit the previous commit: git commit --amend
Edit the previous commit, without updating the message: git commit --amend --no-edit



git status
Check that state of the repository. This will highlight any files that have been edited, any that are not tracked, and any that might already be staged.


git log
Explore the local repository’s history.


git diff
Compare differences across commits.


git push
Upload the work on your local repository to a remote repository.


git fetch / git pull
Download the work on a remote repository to your local repository.

title: Version Control with Git
text:
Writing a commit message

The next person to read your work in 6 months is not going to be some schmuck. It’s going to be YOU!

— A certain UCR Statistics Professor
Treat commit messages like entries in a journal. They are meant to be read by someone. There are two parts of a commit message:

The first line: A succinct summary. This is what gets displayed in most Git tools; e.g. on GitHub.
The rest: Add additional lines to add more context. A commit message can be as long as you want. Use it!

title: Version Control with Git
text:
A basic single user workflow

Using Git for the first time on a new computer

Set up your identity in Git. See Lab 0 on how to configure Git.
Consider setting up a global .gitignore.
Set up SSH access to your GitHub/GitLab/Other Git Service for the new machine.



Setting up a new project

Create the main project directory and cd into it.
Run git init.
Set up the project with some basic files so you can create an initial commit. For example, adding a README.md is a good first step especially if you plan to host the project on GitHub.
Set up a remote repository, if applicable.
Run git add ... and git commit ... to create the first commit in the project.
Push the initial commit to the remote repository.



Working on a project

Run git status to check for local changes. Run git fetch --all to check for remote changes.

If your remote repo has changes, consider whether you can git pull them.

Edit some file(s), working towards The Next Logical Step.

This should be implementing some small part of your project. For example, writing a specific function that your project requires can be The Next Logical Step.
At The Next Logical Step, the project should be in a semi-working state.
In the early phase of a project, that might mean that you’ve worked out enough to test basic functionality.
For example, you might write a script or function to load a dataset and print some summary statistics.

Run git add ... to organize files and changes associated with The Next Logical Step.
Write an informative message about what was done and any useful context.

title: Optimization Examples
text:
using LinearAlgebra, Random, Statistics
using FiniteDifferences, DualNumbers, ForwardDiff
using CSV, DataFrames
using Plots, StatsPlots, LaTeXStrings

title: Optimization Examples
section: Make the problem concrete with data
text:
Make the problem concrete with data
Let’s simulate some data \((y_{i}, \boldsymbol{x}_{i})\):

Set the number of samples \(n = 100\)
Set the number of features to \(p = 2\). We’ll treat \(x_{i1}\) as the intercept “feature” and \(x_{i2}\) as a proper independent variable.
Simulate \(x_{i2} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\), i.e. each instance of the independent variable follows the standard normal distribution.
Set the “ground truth” as \(\beta_{0} = -3\) and \(\beta_{1} = 2\). We’re working with a parametric model so knowing \(\beta\) completely determines the model.
Set \(y_{i} = \boldsymbol{x}_{i}^{\top} \beta + \epsilon_{i} = \beta_{0} + x_{i2} \beta_{1} + \epsilon_{i}\). Here \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) as well.


n = 100
p = 2
X = randn(n, p)
X[:, 1] .= 1
beta = [-3.0, 2.0]
y = X * beta + randn(n)

Remember that in linear regression analysis, we are modeling the conditional mean \(E[Y \mid X] = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1} X\); i.e. \(X\) is given and the goal is to determine \(\beta\) to fully specify the model for the conditional mean.

The simulation above establishes the “ground truth”. We fully simulated the data generating process.
Fitting \(\beta\) using least squares; i.e. \(\rho(r) = \frac{1}{2} r^{2}\) gives a particular estimator.
In principle, we can choose any model for \(\rho(r)\) to fit a model. Optimization + Statistics gives us a way to derive estimators with certain desirable properties.
The OLS estimator gives us the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) for \(\beta\). Follows from Gauss-Markov theorem under certain assumptions. Anything else will be biased in the sense that \(E[\hat{\beta} \mid X] \neq \beta\).


# xmin, xmax = extrema(X[:, 2])
scatter(X[:, 2], y)

title: Optimization Examples
text:
Implement the estimator for OLS
Questions to reflect upon before writing code

What is the optimization model I need to implement? That is, what is the loss/utility function?
What are the required inputs? That is, what information does the caller/user need to tell me?
How do I predict from the statistical model?
How do I measure errors from the model?


function ols_loss(y, X, b)
  # predict from the model
  model_prediction = X * b

  # obtain the residuals
  r = y - model_prediction

  # apply transformation of residuals + aggregrate
  return sum(1/2 * r .^ 2)
end

We wrote a function so let’s test that it does something sensible when we invoke it:

ols_loss(y, X, zeros(2))

This should just be \(\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} y_{i}^2\):

ols_loss(y, X, zeros(2)) ≈ 0.5 * sum(abs2, y) # applies transformation to y[i]'s

Is it compatible with ForwardDiff? After all, we don’t want to spend our lives writing down gradients unless we really need to:

ForwardDiff.gradient(ols_loss, zeros(2)) # won't work

What went wrong???

Start at the top of the message.
Gives us a hopefully informative error.
To find where everything collapsed, look at the stacktrace:

Top: this is the innermost function call (i.e item [1]). Shows types inferred in the function call + line numbers indicating location of error.
Middle: Lots of intermediate function calls.
Bottom: this is the outermost call; usually points to our source code in a Quarto document (or “line” in a REPL).


The error message tells us that Julia cannot evalute ols_loss() as a function of 1 argument. Use an anonymous function to make it a 1 argument function:

ForwardDiff.gradient(b -> ols_loss(y, X, b), zeros(2))


The y and X are implict from the enclosing scope.
Be careful with anonymous functions! In any language, they have a cost paid by the “global” reference.

Doesn’t matter too much in R where function calls are “expensive” anyway.
In Julia this can introduce heavy bottlenecks due to stress applied to its compiler.
Later we’ll see a way to avoid paying the penalty.

title: Optimization Examples
text:
Implement an algorithm
We’ll use gradient descent with a backtracking linesearch.
Before we start writing code

What is the optimization model?
What is the algorithm map?
What assumptions will I make (to simplify coding) and impose on the caller/user?

Outlining the implementation

Our assumptions translate to “interface” in deciding what to put in the function signature.
We started “inside the loop”. How do we stop?

Limit number of iterations.
Check that \(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}) \approx 0\) in some sense. How? Use norm of gradient since \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{v} = 0\).

Semicolon: everything to the right is a keyword argument
Keyword arguments should have type annotations i.e. keyword::SomeType = default_value.
How do we know it’s working? Need to check gradients. \(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}) \approx 0\) is a requirement for a minimum.
for vs while: choice will dictate how you keep track of the algorithm’s state.

Making changes

Generally a good idea to report some information about how well the algorithm performed.

Number of iterations
The solution itself
Gradient or norm of the gradient
Convergence history

Print statements are okay, but users should have a way to disable them. They do incur a cost! Common approach: add a parameter verbose::Bool = false to conditionally print information.
Returning a single “result object” vs a Tuple.

Named tuples are a good compromise.
Avoids the user having to write code like niter, estimate, other_info = solver()
In R, use list() construct. Literally what lm() and similar model fitting functions use to construct reports in the language.



# loss: This is a function-like object, 1-arg, compatible with ForwardDiff
# x0: initial guess
# This function minimizes the loss function and returns the solution x
function gd(loss, x0; maxiter::Int = 100, tol::Real = 1e-3, nsteps::Int = 10)
  # x = x0 # variable assignment
  x = copy(x0) # make a copy of the caller's input
  grad = ForwardDiff.gradient(loss, x) # initialize gradient

  niter = 0
  for iter in 1:maxiter
    niter = iter
    # linesearch
    t = 1.0
    for m in 1:nsteps
      # if we succeed in decreasing the objective
      if loss(x - t * grad) < loss(x)
        break
      else # otherwise
        t = 1/2 * t
      end
    end

    @. x = x - t * grad
    grad .= ForwardDiff.gradient(loss, x) # evaluate gradient at current estimate
    converged = norm(grad) < tol # is gradient close to 0
    if converged
      break # break out of innermost loop
    end
  # not_done = iter < maxiter
  end
  result = (;
    iterations = niter,
    solution = x,
    gradient = grad
  )
  return result
end

We wrote a function, so let’s test it!

loss = b -> ols_loss(y, X, b)
result = gd(loss, zeros(2); maxiter = 100, tol = 1e-3)


Access fields in the NamedTuple with result.<fieldname>; e.g. result.solution delivers the estimate \(\hat{\beta}\).
Close to the ground truth.
Is it a good estimate? Can compare to OLS solution delivered by X \ y. However, sometimes there are no reference tools to compare against.
What would happen if we made the noise terms \(\epsilon_{i}\) large?

title: Optimization Examples
text:
Reflection

The gd() code has little if any problem-specific information contained in it. The function encapsulates the problem of minimizing a loss function.
Similarly, ols_loss() function has little to do with minimization. It simply reports the OLS loss.
In writing good, reusable code we strive for such separation of concerns.
Makes our code composable, especially in a language like Julia.
Same principles apply to writing code for data analysis (vs implementing methodology). Use functions rather than writing large, hard-to-follow scripts.

title: Optimization Examples
section: Try it on a different problem
text:
Try it on a different problem
Implement the Huber loss.

function huber_loss(y, X, b; c = 0.25)
  # predict from the model
  model_prediction = X * b

  # obtain the residuals
  r = y - model_prediction

  # apply transformation of residuals + aggregrate
  tmp = @. ifelse(
    abs(r) <= c,  # condition
    0.5 * r ^ 2,      # if true
    c * (abs(r) - 0.5*c) # if false
  )
  return sum(tmp)
end


Code is very similar to the OLS code.
Only meanginful changes are:

Loss has a parameter c that we should account for. Here we implement it as a keyword argument.
The residual transformation changes slightly.
Challenge: Implement the Huber function efficiently and without the allocation we have above.


We wrote a funciton, so let’s test it.

huber_loss(y, X, zeros(2))

Now test our gd() function on the new problem:

result = gd(b -> huber_loss(y, X, b), zeros(2);
  maxiter = 10 ^ 3,
  tol = 1e-3,
  nsteps = 20
)

In class

Did not converge with maxiter = 10 ^ 2 and nsteps = 10. Suggested that we try a larger iteration budget like maxiter = 10 ^ 3.
Larger iteration budget did not work either. Maybe backtracking was failing, so we try nsteps = 20.
Noticed that gradient was not going towards 0. Points to a problem in our code. Indeed, Dr. Landeros forgot to square r in the abs(r) <= c branch of the code.

title: Optimization Examples
text:
More Reflection

Ideally, we can use a library/package to solve our problem.
HW3 + HW4 should serve as examples to you that developers of stats/ML software cannot address every possible variation of a problem.
Practitioners ((data) scientist, statistician, ML engineer…) need to have some knowledge of algorithms + theory.

Example: How do I know gradient descent will work on my problem?
Example: Do I need a solver with step size control (backtracking)?
Example: Can I design my loss function to be “efficient”, making it easy for AD + black-box solvers to evalute it and its derivaties?
Example: What can I check to make sure an algorithm is working properly on my problem/data?

For us, main takeaway from this exercise is to understand the “levers” we can control in a relatively simple algorithm like gradient descent.

title: Second-Order Methods
text:
using LinearAlgebra, Random, Statistics
using FiniteDifferences, DualNumbers, ForwardDiff
using Plots, LaTeXStrings

title: Second-Order Methods
text:
Newton’s method

Originally developed for finding roots of nonlinear equations\(f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}\).
Newton’s method, aka Newton-Raphson method, is considered the gold standard for its fast (quadratic) convergence \[
  \frac{\|\mathbf{\theta}^{(t+1)} - \mathbf{\theta}^*\|}{\|\mathbf{\theta}^{(t)} - \mathbf{\theta}^*\|^2} \to \text{constant}.
\]
Idea: iterative quadratic approximation.

Taylor expansion around the current iterate \(\mathbf{\theta}^{(t)}\) \[
    L(\mathbf{\theta}) \approx L(\mathbf{\theta}^{(t)}) + \nabla L(\mathbf{\theta}^{(t)})^T (\mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{\theta}^{(t)}) + \frac 12 (\mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{\theta}^{(t)})^T [\nabla^2L(\mathbf{\theta}^{(t)})] (\mathbf{\theta} - \mathbf{\theta}^{(t)})
\] and then maximize the quadratic approximation. To maximize the quadratic function, we set its gradient to zero \[
    \nabla L(\theta^{(t)}) + [\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})] (\theta - \theta^{(t)}) = \mathbf{0}_p,
\] which suggests the next iterate \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    \theta^{(t+1)} &=& \theta^{(t)} - [\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)}) \\
    &=& \theta^{(t)} + [-\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)}).
\end{eqnarray*}
\] This is a naive Newton’s method, because as we saw last time, the search direction \([-\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})\) may overshoot.
There is also a stability issue. Naive Newton’s iterate is not guaranteed to be an ascent algorithm. It’s equally happy to head uphill or downhill. Following example shows that the Newton iterate converges to a local maximum, converges to a local minimum, or diverges depending on starting points.

using Plots; gr()
using LaTeXStrings, ForwardDiff

f(x) = sin(x)
df  = x -> ForwardDiff.derivative(f, x) # gradient
d2f = x -> ForwardDiff.derivative(df, x) # hessian
x = 2.0 # start point: 2.0 (local maximum), 2.75 (diverge), 4.0 (local minimum)
titletext = "Starting point: $x"
anim = @animate for iter in 0:10
    iter > 0 && (global x = x - d2f(x) \ df(x))
    p = Plots.plot(f, 0, 2π, xlim=(0, 2π), ylim=(-1.1, 1.1), legend=nothing, title=titletext)
    Plots.plot!(p, [x], [f(x)], shape=:circle)
    Plots.annotate!(p, x, f(x), text(latexstring("x^{($iter)}"), :right))
end
gif(anim, "./tmp.gif", fps = 1);

  
Remedies for the instability issue:

approximate \(-\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})\) by a positive definite \(\mathbf{A}\) (if it’s not), and
line search (backtracking).

Why do we insist on a positive definite approximation of Hessian? By first-order Taylor expansion, \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    & & L(\theta^{(t)} + s \Delta \theta^{(t)}) - L(\theta^{(t)}) \\
    &=& L(\theta^{(t)}) + s \cdot \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})^T \Delta \theta^{(t)} + o(s) - L(\theta^{(t)}) \\
    &=& s \cdot \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})^T \Delta \theta^{(t)} + o(s) \\
    &=& s \cdot \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})^T [\mathbf{A}^{(t)}]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)}) + o(s).
\end{eqnarray*}
\]
For \(s\) sufficiently small, right hand side is strictly positive when \(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\) is positive definite. The quantity \(\{\nabla L(\theta^{(t)})^T [\mathbf{A}^{(t)}]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})\}^{1/2}\) is termed the Newton decrement.
In summary, a practical Newton-type algorithm iterates according to
\[
    \boxed{ \theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)} + s [\mathbf{A}^{(t)}]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})
    = \theta^{(t)} + s \Delta \theta^{(t)} }
\] where \(\mathbf{A}^{(t)}\) is a pd approximation of \(-\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})\) and \(s\) is a step length.

For strictly concave \(L\), \(-\nabla^2L(\theta^{(t)})\) is always positive definite. Line search is still needed to guarantee convergence.
Line search strategy: step-halving (\(s=1,1/2,\ldots\)), golden section search, cubic interpolation, Amijo rule, … Note the Newton direction
\[
\Delta \theta^{(t)} = [\mathbf{A}^{(t)}]^{-1} \nabla L(\theta^{(t)})
\] only needs to be calculated once. Cost of line search mainly lies in objective function evaluation.
How to approximate \(-\nabla^2L(\theta)\)? More of an art than science. Often requires problem specific analysis.
Taking \(\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}\) leads to the method of steepest ascent, aka gradient ascent.

title: Second-Order Methods
text:
Generalized linear model (GLM)

Logistic regression
Let’s consider a concrete example: logistic regression.

The goal is to predict whether a credit card transaction is fraud (\(y_i=1\)) or not (\(y_i=0\)). Predictors (\(\mathbf{x}_i\)) include: time of transaction, last location, merchant, …
\(y_i \in \{0,1\}\), \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{p}\). Model $y_i \(Bernoulli\)(p_i)$.
Logistic regression. Density \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
  f(y_i|p_i) &=& p_i^{y_i} (1-p_i)^{1-y_i} \\
  &=& e^{y_i \ln p_i + (1-y_i) \ln (1-p_i)} \\
  &=& e^{y_i \ln \frac{p_i}{1-p_i} + \ln (1-p_i)},
\end{eqnarray*}
\] where \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \mathbf{E} (y_i) = p_i &=& \frac{e^{\eta_i}}{1+ e^{\eta_i}} \quad \text{(mean function, inverse link function)} \\
  \eta_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T \beta &=& \ln \left( \frac{p_i}{1-p_i} \right) \quad \text{(logit link function)}.
\end{eqnarray*}
\]
Given data \((y_i,\mathbf{x}_i)\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\),

\[
\begin{eqnarray*}
    L_n(\beta) &=& \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \ln p_i + (1-y_i) \ln (1-p_i) \right] \\
    &=& \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ y_i \mathbf{x}_i^T \beta - \ln (1 + e^{\mathbf{x}_i^T \beta}) \right] \\
    \nabla L_n(\beta) &=& \sum_{i=1}^n \left( y_i \mathbf{x}_i - \frac{e^{\mathbf{x}_i^T \beta}}{1+e^{\mathbf{x}_i^T \beta}} \mathbf{x}_i \right) \\
    &=& \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - p_i) \mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p})  \\
    - \nabla^2L_n(\beta) &=& \sum_{i=1}^n p_i(1-p_i) \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^T = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{X}, \quad
    \text{where } \mathbf{W} &=& \text{diag}(w_1,\ldots,w_n), w_i = p_i (1-p_i) \\
    \mathbf{FIM}_n(\beta) &=& \mathbf{E} [- \nabla^2L_n(\beta)] = - \nabla^2L_n(\beta).
\end{eqnarray*}
\]

Newton’s method == Fisher’s scoring iteration: \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
  \beta^{(t+1)} &=& \beta^{(t)} + s[-\nabla^2 L(\beta^{(t)})]^{-1} \nabla L(\beta^{(t)})  \\
  &=& \beta^{(t)} + s(\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W}^{(t)} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}^{(t)}) \\
  &=& (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W}^{(t)} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W}^{(t)} \left[ \mathbf{X} \beta^{(t)} + s(\mathbf{W}^{(t)})^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}^{(t)}) \right] \\
  &=& (\mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W}^{(t)} \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W}^{(t)} \mathbf{z}^{(t)},
\end{eqnarray*}
\] where \[
  \mathbf{z}^{(t)} = \mathbf{X} \beta^{(t)} + s(\mathbf{W}^{(t)})^{-1} (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{p}^{(t)})
\] are the working responses. A Newton’s iteration is equivalent to solving a weighed least squares problem \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i (z_i - \mathbf{x}_i^T \beta)^2\). Thus the name IRWLS (iteratively re-weighted least squares).



GLM
Let’s consider the more general class of generalized linear models (GLM).








Family
Canonical Link
Variance Function




Normal
\(\eta=\mu\)
1


Poisson
\(\eta=\log \mu\)
\(\mu\)


Binomial
\(\eta=\log \left( \frac{\mu}{1 - \mu} \right)\)
\(\mu (1 - \mu)\)


Gamma
\(\eta = \mu^{-1}\)
\(\mu^2\)


Inverse Gaussian
\(\eta = \mu^{-2}\)
\(\mu^3\)




\(Y\) belongs to an exponential family with density \[
  p(y|\theta,\phi) = \exp \left\{ \frac{y\theta - b(\theta)}{a(\phi)} + c(y,\phi) \right\}.
\]

\(\theta\): natural parameter.

\(\phi>0\): dispersion parameter.
GLM relates the mean \(\mu = \mathbf{E}(Y|\mathbf{x})\) via a strictly increasing link function \[
  g(\mu) = \eta = \mathbf{x}^T \beta, \quad \mu = g^{-1}(\eta)
\]

Score, Hessian, information

\[\begin{eqnarray*}
    \nabla L_n(\beta) &=& \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i-\mu_i) \mu_i'(\eta_i)}{\sigma_i^2} \mathbf{x}_i \\
    \,- \nabla^2 L_n(\boldsymbol{\beta}) &=& \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{[\mu_i'(\eta_i)]^2}{\sigma_i^2} \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^T - \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu_i) \mu_i''(\eta_i)}{\sigma_i^2} \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^T \\
  & & + \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{(y_i - \mu_i) [\mu_i'(\eta_i)]^2 (d \sigma_i^{2} / d\mu_i)}{\sigma_i^4} \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^T \\
    \mathbf{FIM}_n(\beta) &=& \mathbf{E} [- \nabla^2 L_n(\beta)] = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{[\mu_i^{\prime}(\eta_i)]^2}{\sigma_i^2} \mathbf{x}_i \mathbf{x}_i^T = \mathbf{X}^T \mathbf{W} \mathbf{X}.
\end{eqnarray*}\]

Fisher scoring method \[
  \beta^{(t+1)} = \beta^{(t)} + s [\mathbf{FIM}(\beta^{(t)})]^{-1} \nabla L_n(\beta^{(t)})
\]

Amounts to IRWLS with weights \(w_i = [\mu_i^{\prime}(\eta_i)]^2/\sigma_i^2\) and some working responses \(z_i\).

For canonical link, \(\theta = \eta\), the second term of Hessian vanishes and Hessian coincides with Fisher information matrix. Convex problem 😄 \[
  \text{Fisher's scoring == Newton's method}.
\]
Non-canonical link, non-convex problem 😞 \[
  \text{Fisher's scoring algorithm} \ne \text{Newton's method}.
\] Example: Probit regression (binary response with probit link). \[
\begin{eqnarray*}
  y_i &\sim& \text{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\
  p_i &=& \Phi(\mathbf{x}_i^T \beta)  \\
  \eta_i &=& \mathbf{x}_i^T \beta = \Phi^{-1}(p_i).
\end{eqnarray*}
\] where \(\Phi(\cdot)\) is the cdf of a standard normal.
Julia, R and Matlab implement the Fisher scoring method, aka IRWLS, for GLMs.

GLM.jl package.

title: Second-Order Methods
text:
Score + Information
Score:
\[
\nabla f(\beta) = - \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}, \beta)) \nabla \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}, \beta)
\]
Hessian:
\[
\nabla^{2}f(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \nabla \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i},\beta) \nabla \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}, \beta)^{\top}
-
\sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_{i} - \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}, \beta)) \nabla^{2} \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i},\beta)
\]
Fisher Information:
\[
\mathrm{FIM}(\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \nabla \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i},\beta) \nabla \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{i}, \beta)^{\top} = \boldsymbol{J}(\beta)^{\top}\boldsymbol{J}(\beta),
\]
with \(\boldsymbol{J}(\beta)^{\top} = [\mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{1},\beta), \ldots, \mu(\boldsymbol{x}_{n}, \beta)] \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times n}\).

title: Second-Order Methods
text:
Example: Curve Fitting
For an example, consider the logistic growth model used and studied in the sciences:
\[
\mu(x,\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\beta_{3}) = \frac{\beta_{3}}{1 + e^{-\beta_{1} - \beta_{2}x}}
\]

logistic_growth(b, x) = b[3] / (1 + exp(-b[1] - b[2]*x))


Random.seed!(206)

b0 = [4.0, 0.5, 1e3]
x = range(0, 10, step = 0.2)
y = map(xi -> logistic_growth(b0, xi) + randn(), x)

fig = scatter(x, y; label = "Data", xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Population Size")


function nonlin_reg_loss(f, b, y, x)
  yhat = map(xi -> f(b, xi), x)
  return 1 / 2 * sum((y - yhat) .^ 2)
end


nonlin_reg_loss(logistic_growth, ones(3), y, x)


b = 10*rand(3)
f = params -> nonlin_reg_loss(logistic_growth, params, y, x)
g = logistic_growth
f_old = f(b)
Jt = zeros(3, length(y))
for iter in 1:10^3
  score = ForwardDiff.gradient(f, b)
  @views for i in axes(Jt, 2)
    ForwardDiff.gradient!(Jt[:, i], params -> g(params, x[i]), b)
  end
  H = Jt * transpose(Jt) + 1e-3*I
  d = H \ score
  s = 1.0
  while f(b - s * d) > f_old
    s = s / 2
  end
  @. b = b - s * d
  f_old = f(b)
end

display(b)


plot!(fig, x, x -> logistic_growth(b, x), label = "Fitted", color = :red)

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
using LinearAlgebra, Random, Statistics
using FiniteDifferences, DualNumbers, ForwardDiff
using Plots, LaTeXStrings

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Hierarchy of Optimization Methods

Zero Order: Use only function values, \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\), to solve the problem. Used if \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\) does not have a sensible derivative or gradients are too costly to evaluate. Usually check \(|f(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}) - f(\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1})| < \epsilon\); i.e. function values have converged.

Nelder-Mead
Approximate Gradient Descent (i.e. using finite differences)
Random Coordinate Descent

First Order: Uses at most information from first derivatives, \(f(\boldsymbol{x})\); i.e. directions of ascent/descent. Usually check \(\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1})\| \le \epsilon\); i.e. gradient is sufficiently small.

Gradient Descent (for certain choices of step size)
Stochastic Gradient Descent (ditto)
Mirror Descent
ADMM (Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers)


Notion of derivative not limited to the “usual” definition; also covers subgradient and other weak notions of derivative.

Second Order: Uses at most information from second derivatives, \(d^{2}f(\boldsymbol{x})\); i.e. curvature.

Newton’s Method
Fisher Scoring
Coordinate Descent?


Common in scientific computing, even for “large” scale problems. Conspicuously absent in (deep) machine learning. Advances in randomized linear algebra may change this.

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Naive Approach
The (naive) gradient descent approach is simply
\[
\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = \boldsymbol{x}_{k} - \nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}).
\]
Without any restrictions on the gradient, it becomes possible for the method to overshoot and thus fail to converge, even when the underlying function is easy to minimize.

myfun(x) = (x - 1)^2

function gradient_descent_example(x0, t::Real = 1.0)
  x = x0
  history_x = [x0]
  for i in 1:10
    x = x - t * ForwardDiff.derivative(myfun, x)
    push!(history_x, x)
  end

  @show history_x

  fig = plot(range(-3, 4, step = 0.25), myfun, label = L"f(x)", lw = 3)
  plot!(history_x, myfun.(history_x), label = "History", lw = 3, ls = :dash)
  return fig
end

Starting from \(x_{0} = 3.0\):

gradient_descent_example(3.0)

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Fixed Step Size
Amend the gradient descent updates with a step size that indicates how far along to move in the direction \(\boldsymbol{d}\):
\[
\boldsymbol{x}_{k+1} = \boldsymbol{x}_{k} - t \nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}_{k}).
\]
This changes little in determining \(\boldsymbol{d}\) if we are happy to simply take \(t\) to be a fixed value.

gradient_descent_example(3.0, 0.9)


gradient_descent_example(3.0, 0.5)

Why does the choice \(t = 0.5\) lead to an algorithm that converges in one step?

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Exact
The exact line search problem is
\[
\min_{s,~s \ge 0}~f(\boldsymbol{x} + s \boldsymbol{d}),
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{d}\) are fixed beforehand. The goal is to have \(f(\boldsymbol{x} + s \boldsymbol{d}) < f(\boldsymbol{x})\). This problem is intractable except in the simplest of problems; e.g. for a quadratic or a Lipschitz-smooth \(f\) more generally.
Lipschitz continuity:
There exists \(L > 0\) such that for every \(x,y\) the following inequality holds:
\[
\|f(x) - f(y)\| \le L \|x - y\|.
\]
This is a statement about how large derivatives can become and defines a global property of a function. To see this, rearrange:
\[
\frac{\|f(x) - f(y)\|}{\|x - y\|} \le L
\]
Lipschitz smoothness:
Same as above, except the statement is about gradients of functions.
\[
\|\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}) - f(\boldsymbol{y})\| \le L \|\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\|
\]

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Backtracking
Exact line searches rarely have closed form solutions. Even when th problem is tractable, it may be expensive to compute the step size exactly.
What is done in practice is a backtracking line search. The idea is simple:

Propose an initial step size \(t \leftarrow 1\).
Apply the (gradient descent) update, \(x \leftarrow x + td\).
Check that a descent condition holds; for example, \(f(x + td) < f(x)\).

If the descent condition fails, undo the update and set \(t \leftarrow \alpha t\) for \(\alpha \in (0, 1)\). Go back to Step 2 with the new step size.

Continue with gradient descent.

A common choice for \(\alpha\) is \(\alpha = \frac{1}{2}\). This flavor of backtracking is known as step halving.

Example: Gradient Descent + Backtracking

function rosenbrock(x)
  return (1 - x[1]) ^ 2 + 100 * (x[2] - x[1] ^ 2) ^ 2
end


xs = range(-2, 2, step = 0.1)
ys = range(-1, 3, step = 0.1)
contourf(xs, ys, (x, y) -> log10(1e-6 + rosenbrock([x,y])), color = :plasma, levels = 64, lw = 0)


function gradient_descent(f, x0; maxiter::Int = 10, tol::Real = 1e-3, backtracking::Bool = false, t::Real = 0.1)
  # initialize our workspace
  x = copy(x0)
  ∇f = similar(x)

  # initial function + gradient values
  f_old = f(x)
  ForwardDiff.gradient!(∇f, f, x)

  # start the minimization loop
  not_converged = norm(∇f) > tol
  iter = 0
  while not_converged && iter < maxiter
    iter += 1
    if backtracking
      # try a full step
      t = 1.0
      @. x = x - t * ∇f
      while f(x) >= f_old # backtracking
        @. x = x + t * ∇f
        t = t / 2
        @. x = x - t * ∇f
      end
      f_old = f(x)
    else # fixed step size
      @. x = x - t * ∇f
    end
    # check convergence
    ForwardDiff.gradient!(∇f, f, x)
    not_converged = norm(∇f) > tol
  end
  ForwardDiff.gradient!(∇f, f, x)
  return iter, x, f(x), norm(∇f)
end


gradient_descent(rosenbrock, [1.5, 1.5], maxiter = 10^4, backtracking = false)


gradient_descent(rosenbrock, [1.5, 1.5], maxiter = 10^4, backtracking = true)

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Other Descent Conditions
Knowledge of more complex descent conditions can improve convergence behavior of a first-order method. Requires some additional background to understand.

Armijo: Defines sufficient decrease.
Wolfe: Armijo + curvature condition.

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Implementation

f(params, data): Assumed to be a function-like object that accepts two arguments: a vector of parameters params and data, given as a Tuple of the form (y, X).
x0: Starting estimate.
batchfun(): A zero-argument function that returns a random batch from the problem’s training data.


function sgd(f, x0, batchfun; maxiter::Int = 10, tol::Real = 1e-3, batchsize::Int = 10)
  # initialize our workspace
  x = copy(x0)
  ∇f, ∇ftmp = similar(x), similar(x)

  # helper function to evaluate gradient on mini-batch
  # note the variables folded into the function definition
  function eval_gradient!(x, batch)
    fill!(∇f, 0)
    for obs in zip(batch[1], eachrow(batch[2]))
      ForwardDiff.gradient!(∇ftmp, params -> f(params, obs), x)
      @. ∇f += ∇ftmp
    end
    @. ∇f = 1 / batchsize * ∇f
    return ∇f
  end

  # initial batch, function + gradient values
  batch = batchfun(batchsize)
  f_old = f(x, batch)
  eval_gradient!(x, batch)

  # start the minimization loop
  not_converged = norm(∇f) > tol
  iter = 0
  while not_converged && iter < maxiter
    iter += 1
    t = 1 / iter
    @. x = x - t * ∇f

    # check convergence
    eval_gradient!(x, batch)
    not_converged = norm(∇f) > tol

    # update the batch
    not_converged && (batch = batchfun(batchsize))
  end
  eval_gradient!(x, batch)
  return iter, x, f(x, batch), norm(∇f)
end







NoteChoosing the Step Size



This implementation uses dimishing step sizes, \(1 / k\). Lot’s of other schemes in literature; fixed step sizes will not work.

title: First-Order Methods”
text:
Example: Linear Regression

function simulate_linreg_problem(n, β0, σ; rng = Random.default_rng())
  X = Matrix{Float64}(undef, n, 2)
  @views begin
    fill!(X[:, 1], 1)
    randn!(rng, X[:, 2])
    X[:, 2] .= X[:, 2]
  end
  y = X * β0 .+ σ * randn(rng, n)
  return y, X
end


y, X = simulate_linreg_problem(10 ^ 4, [0.5, -3.0], 1/sqrt(2));

fig = scatter(X[:, 2], y,
  xlabel = "X (Independent)",
  ylabel = "y (Dependent)",
  label = "Data",
  alpha = 0.25,
  markerstrokewidth = 0
)


Step 1: Define the Loss
Remember that ForwarDiff asks that the functions we differentiate only have one argument. If we have multiple parameters, they must be packed into a Vector.
With this in mind, let’s make the coefficients b the first argument below.

function linreg_loss(b, y, X::AbstractMatrix)
  r = y - X*b
  return 1/2 * mean(abs2, r)
end

linreg_loss(b, y, x::AbstractVector) = 1/2 * (y - dot(x, b)) ^ 2


linreg_loss([0.0, 0.0], y, X) # make sure it works!


linreg_loss([0.5, -3.0], y, X)

For compatibility with ForwardDiff, we just use an anonymous function

ForwardDiff.gradient(b -> linreg_loss(b, y, X), zeros(2))



Step 2: Define the Sampling Procedure
Let’s use a batch of fixed size. The following function explicitly requires 3 arguments to sample from (y, X).

function mybatchfun(y, X, batchsize)
  idx = rand(1:length(y), batchsize)
  return y[idx], X[idx, :]
end


yb, Xb = mybatchfun(y, X, 10)
display(yb)
display(Xb)

Other possible schemes:

Sample a single observation
Cyclic: Shuffle data, then iterate over data using a fixed sized window.



Step 3: Ensure compatibility
To make the output of batchfun() compatible with our loss function, add a method that expands the second argument to y and X.

linreg_loss(b, data::Tuple) = linreg_loss(b, data[1], data[2])

Make sure it works:

linreg_loss(zeros(2), mybatchfun(y, X, 10))

Need compatibility with ForwardDiff.gradient(), too:

abatch = mybatchfun(y, X, 10)
ForwardDiff.gradient(y -> linreg_loss(y, abatch), zeros(2))



Step 4: Test It

iter, β, loss, grad = @time gradient_descent(
  b -> linreg_loss(b, y, X), # function of parameters; using full data
  zeros(2);
  maxiter = 10^3,
  tol = 1e-6,
  backtracking = true
)
println("""
Gradient Descent
  - Iterations: $(iter)
  - Estimate: $(β)
  - Loss: $(loss)
  - Gradient Norm: $(grad)
""")
plot!(fig, range(-4, 4), x -> β[1] + x*β[2], color = :black, label = "GD", lw = 3, ls = :dash);


Random.seed!(206)
iter, β, loss, grad = @time sgd(
  linreg_loss,              # function of parameters + data
  zeros(2),
  b -> mybatchfun(y, X, b); # function of batch size
  maxiter = 10^4,
  tol = 1e-3,
  batchsize = 50
)
println("""
Stochastic Gradient Descent
  - Iterations: $(iter)
  - Estimate: $(β)
  - Loss: $(loss)
  - Gradient Norm: $(grad)
""")
plot!(fig, range(-4, 4), x -> β[1] + x*β[2], color = :red, label = "SGD", lw = 3, ls = :dot);


fig


linreg_loss(β, y, X) # full data

A. A Custom Matrix Type
The code below defines a type PageRankPImPt, which consists of a connectivity matrix A, a teleportation parameter p, and a few additional arrays needed for the sparse + low rank representation. Below it is a constructor that tells Julia how to build an instance of PageRankPImPt given a particular set of imputs. Note that we subtype AbstractMatrix{T}, indicating that the object will behave like a Matrix.
Finish implementing the constructor code so that it produces a valid representation of \(\mathbf{P}\).

# a type for the matrix M = I - Pᵀ in the PageRank problem
struct PageRankImPt{TA <: Number, IA <: Integer, T <: AbstractFloat} <: AbstractMatrix{T}
  A :: SparseMatrixCSC{TA, IA}  # adjacency matrix
  p :: T                        # teleportation parameter
  d :: Vector{T}                # :)
  v :: Vector{T}                # :)
  tmp :: Vector{T}              # storage for any intermediates
end

# constructor: using only A and p
function PageRankImPt(A::SparseMatrixCSC, p::T) where T <: AbstractFloat
  n = size(A, 1)
  d = similar(Vector{T}, n)
  v = similar(Vector{T}, n)
  tmp = similar(Vector{T}, n)
  # TODO: Fill d and v with appropriate values
  return PageRankImPt(A, p, d, v, tmp)
end

Instructions

This problem set contains 7 problems. Each problem must be completed for full credit.
You are encouraged to work with other students. Clearly identify your collaborators by naming them in the author field in the front matter.
This assignment will guide you in implementing NNMF, testing it, and applying it to a real dataset.
Computational efficiency, in terms of speed and memory, is a key criterion in grading this assignment.



Overview
Nonnegative matrix factorization (NNMF) was introduced by Lee and Seung (1999) as an alternative to principal components and vector quantization. This method appeared in the past (Lawton and Sylvestre, 1971) as a technique for determining the shape of two overlapping functions via additive mixtures. Today, NNMF has applications in data compression, clustering, and deconvolution.






Figure 1: Illustration of NNMF



In mathematical terms, the goal of NNMF is to approximate a data matrix \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) with nonnegative entries \(x_{ij}\) as a product of two low-rank matrices \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}\) and \(\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times n}\), also with nonnegative entries \(v_{ik}\) and \(w_{kj}\). That is, one chooses \(r < \min\{m,n\}\) so that the rank of \(\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) is at most \(r\). We fit/estimate the factors \(\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) by minimizing the squared Frobenius norm of the residuals matrix \(\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{V} \mathbf{W}\), \[
L(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{W}) = \|\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{V} \mathbf{W}\|_{\text{F}}^2 = \sum_i \sum_j \left(x_{ij} - \sum_k v_{ik} w_{kj} \right)^2, \quad v_{ik} \ge 0, w_{kj} \ge 0,
\] which should lead to a good factorization. Lee and Seung suggest an iterative algorithm with multiplicative updates \[
v_{ik}^{(t+1)} = v_{ik}^{(t)} \frac{\sum_j x_{ij} w_{kj}^{(t)}}{\sum_j b_{ij}^{(t)} w_{kj}^{(t)}}, \quad \text{where } b_{ij}^{(t)} = \sum_k v_{ik}^{(t)} w_{kj}^{(t)},
\] \[
w_{kj}^{(t+1)} = w_{kj}^{(t)} \frac{\sum_i x_{ij} v_{ik}^{(t+1)}}{\sum_i b_{ij}^{(t+1/2)} v_{ik}^{(t+1)}}, \quad \text{where } b_{ij}^{(t+1/2)} = \sum_k v_{ik}^{(t+1)} w_{kj}^{(t)}
\] that will drive the objective \(L^{(t)} = L(\mathbf{V}^{(t)}, \mathbf{W}^{(t)})\) downhill. Superscript \(t\) indicates the iteration number.


Problem 1: Check Your Understanding
Before we code anything, let’s make sure we have a conceptual understanding of the method. Refer to the abstract of Lee and Seung (1999) and Figure 1. Answer the following questions:

Based on Figure 1, what do the rows of \(\mathbf{X}\) represent?
What about the columns of \(\mathbf{X}\)?
The factors \(\mathbf{V}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) are rank \(r\), with \(r\) typically smaller than \(m\) and \(n\). As such, this reduces the amount memory required to store \(\mathbf{X}\) albeit with a small loss of information. Based on the previous two questions, which matrix (\(\mathbf{V}\) or \(\mathbf{W}\)) encodes the original images?
Using your previous answer, which matrix represents a ‘dictionary’, ‘mapping’, or ‘coordinate system’ that helps us approximate the original image from its compressed representation?
Suppose you have \(50,000\) images that are each \(128 \times 128\) pixels large, and you find a rank \(1000\) approximation that is ‘good enough’. Assuming pixels are stored as Float64 (8 bytes), how much savings in memory is achieved with NNMF? Justify your answer.



Problem 2: Implementation
Implement Lee and Seung’s algorithm based on the following inputs:

\(\mathbf{X}\) (data, each row is a vectorized image)
rank \(r\),
convergence tolerance,
and optional starting point \((\mathbf{V}^{(0)}, \mathbf{W}^{(0)})\).

Use the template below to help you get started.

Problem 3: Inspecting Data
The MIT Center for Biological and Computational Learning (CBCL) used to maintain a famous datset of face images. The database reduces to a matrix \(\mathbf{X}\) containing \(m = 2,429\) gray-scale face images with \(n = 19 \times 19 = 361\) pixels per face. Each image (row) is scaled to have mean and standard deviation 0.25.
Read in the nnmf-2429-by-361-face.txt file posted on Canvas, e.g., using the readdlm() function, and display a few sample images, e.g., using the Images.jl package.


Problem 4: Correctness and Efficiency
Report the run times, using @btime, of your function for fitting NNMF on the MIT CBCL face data set at ranks \(r=10, 20, 30, 40, 50\). For ease of comparison and grading, please start your algorithm with the provided \(\mathbf{V}^{(0)}\) (first \(r\) columns of V0.txt) and \(\mathbf{W}^{(0)}\) (first \(r\) rows of W0.txt). \[

\]

title: Automatic Differentiation
text:
Dual Numbers
Before we look at AD let’s examine a curious extension of the real line \(\mathbb{R}\), the dual numbers. Dual numbers define a number system with infinitesimals \(\epsilon\) such that \(\epsilon^{2} = 0\) *by definition. Given a real number \(x\), one constructs its associated dual number by \(x + \epsilon\). The utility of dual numbers is that evaluating functions over dual numbers immediately yields function values and derivatives simultaneously. For example, consider \(f(x) = x^2\). Evaluation of \(f\) over dual numbers yields
\[
f(x + \epsilon) = (x + \epsilon)^2 = x^2 + 2x\epsilon + \epsilon^2 = x^{2} + 2x\epsilon = f(x) + f^{\prime}(x)\epsilon.
\]
The real part of the dual number is simply the value \(f(x)\), whereas the dual part accumulates \(f^{\prime}(x)\). The technique generalizes to more complicated functions and extens to vector-valued functions in general. The ForwardDiff documentation has excellent explanations on the mathematical and implementation details.
This may sound too good to be true! Extensions of the real line using infinitesimals was formalized by the logician Abraham Robinson. Dual numbers and forward-mode AD are not merely curious computational tricks.

function rosenbrock(x)
  return (1 - x[1]) ^ 2 + 100 * (x[2] - x[1] ^ 2) ^ 2
end


xs = ys = range(-3, 3, length = 101)
tv = -4:4
tl = [L"10^{%$i}" for i in tv]
contourf(xs, ys, (x, y) -> log10(rosenbrock([x, y]));
  levels = 16,
  color = :plasma,
  xlabel = L"x_{1}",
  ylabel = L"x_{2}",
  colorbar_ticks = (tv, tl),
  title = "Rosenbrock Function"
)


ForwardDiff.gradient(rosenbrock, Float64[1, 1]) # gradient at minimum

title: Optimization Intro
text:
Many problems in statistics come down to optimization (but not all of them).
So do lots of problems in economics, physics, CS, biology, operations research …
Mathematical optimization deals in minimums \(\min\) and maximums \(\max\).
Statisticians usually talk about maximization; the field of optimization often just study minimization. We translate one to the other with minus signs.

Lots of estimators are formulated in terms of minimization/maximization.

Ordinary least squares (including variants with ridge, lasso, elastic net…)
Least angle regression (LARS); OLS but with \(|\cdot|\)
Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)
Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation; Bayesian statistics
Machine learning: loss + regularization

title: Optimization Intro
text:
Example: The Babylonian Method
The ancient Babylonians knew how to approximate the hypotenuse of a triangle, which involves computing the square root of a non-negative number. The Greek mathematician Heron would later define an explicit algorithm for computing the square root of an arbitrary non-negative number \(c\), which is often attributed to the Babylonians due to their geometric skills.
Source: Babylonian Method (Wikipedia)
Credit: Algorithms from THE BOOK (Chapter 1, Section 3)
Before seeing the algorithm, let us first formulate the problem precisely: Given \(c > 0\), we seek a number \(x\) such that \(x = \sqrt{c}\). A little rearranging reveals the generic problem:
\[
f(x) = x^{2} - c = 0; \qquad c > 0,
\]
that is, we need to find a root or zero of the function \(f(x) = x^{2} - c\).
From elementary calculus, we know our objective \(f(x)\) is differentiable and that we can approximate the objective’s value at \(x\) from its properties at an anchor point \(x_{0}\). To first order, Taylor’s theorem states we can extrapolate from \(x_{0}\) via
\[
f(x) = f(x_{0}) + f^{\prime}(x_{0})(x - x_{0}) + O(|x-x_{0}|^{2}).
\]
Assume this approximation is good enough, i.e. the \(O(|x-x_{0}|^{2})\) terms is negligible. Focus on the linear piece only; this simply defines a line with \(y = f(x)\):
\[
y = f(x_{0}) + f^{\prime}(x_{0})(x - x_{0}).
\]
The derivative \(f^{\prime}(x_{0})\) defines its slope. To determine its \(x\)-intercept, we solve by finding \(x_{1}\) such that \(y = 0\):
\[
0 = f(x_{0}) + f^{\prime}(x_{0})(x_{1} - x_{0}),
\]
which yields
\[
x_{1} = x_{0} - \frac{f(x_{0})}{f^{\prime}(x_{0})}.
\]
This provides a generic recipe for extrapolating \(x\)-intercepts for the lines \(y = f(x_{n}) + f^{\prime}(x_{n})(x - x_{n})\) where \(y = f(x)\). Thus, iterating the algorithm map
\[
x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{f(x_{n})}{f^{\prime}(x_{n})},
\]
should, under certain conditions, recover an estimate \(x\) such that \(f(x) = 0\). Filling in the details for our problem, we have
\[
x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{x_{n}^{2} - c}{2 x_{n}}.
\]
This is precisely the Newton-Raphson method for calculating roots of functions. It requires \(f(x)\) to be differentiable with respect to \(x\). Later we will see a version of Newton-Raphson for optimization.

title: Optimization Intro
section: Solve as a Root Finding Problem
text:
Solve as a Root Finding Problem
The method turns out to be the so-called Babylonian method to estimate square roots. After some rearrangement, recipe is
\[
x_{n+1} = \frac{1}{2} \left[x_{n}+\frac{c}{x_{n}}\right].
\]
This is an iterative algorithm in which the next iterate (left-hand side), \(x_{n+1}\), is defined by some function of the previous iterates (just \(x_{n}\) in this case) plus some additional problem data (such as the number, \(c\)).
The following code implements the algorithm using the stopping condition \(|x_{n+1}^{2} - c| < \epsilon\) for some tolerance parameter \(\epsilon\).


Code
function babylonian(c, x0; maxiter = 10, epsilon = 1e-3)
  not_converged = c != 0              # convergence check
  x = ifelse(not_converged, x0, c)    # current estimate
  n = 0                               # iteration counter
  while (not_converged && n < maxiter)
    x = 0.5 * (x + c / x)                   # update
    not_converged = abs(x^2 - c) > epsilon  # check
    n = n + 1                               # update counter
  end
  status = ifelse(not_converged, "did not", "did")
  println("The algorithm ", status, " converge after ", n, " iterations.")
  return x
end



babylonian(pi, 3.14, epsilon = 1e-6) - sqrt(pi)

title: Optimization Intro
text:
Solve as a Minimization Problem
Alternatively, we can cast the problem of calculating square roots as an optimization problem. That is, minimize the residual in
\[
f(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x^{2} - c)^2
\]

Why the square? Large negative values should be penalized just as much as large positive values. Absolute values are not differentiable, but squares are.
Want \(x^{2}\) “close” to \(c\); that is, in terms of squared Euclidean distance. Generalize to \(d\) dimensions.
Probably not the best idea here.

From calculus we know that the stationary condition \(f^{\prime}(x) = 0\) indicates a critical point. Thus, we might think to apply the root-finding Newton-Raphson method to the function \(f^{\prime}(x)\). This leads to the algorithm map
\[
x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{f^{\prime}(x_{n})}{f^{\prime\prime}(x_{n})},
\]
which requires \(f(x)\) to be twice-differentiable. Filling in the details, we have
\[
x_{n+1} = x_{n} - \frac{x_{n}(x_{n}^{2} - c)}{3 x^{2}_{n} -c}
\]


Code
function newton_sqrt(c, x0; maxiter = 10, epsilon = 1e-3)
  not_converged = c != 0
  x = ifelse(not_converged, x0, c)
  n = 0
  while (not_converged && n < maxiter)
    x2 = x*x
    x = x - x * (x2 - c) / (3 * x2 - c)
    not_converged = abs(x^2 - c) > epsilon  # check
    n = n + 1
  end
  status = ifelse(not_converged, "did not", "did")
  println("The algorithm ", status, " converge after ", n, " iterations.")
  return x
end



newton_sqrt(pi, 3.14, epsilon = 1e-6) - sqrt(pi)

title: Optimization Intro
text:
Definitions
Functions of several variables have many notions of derivatives.
For a function \(f : \mathbb{R}^{d} \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}\), define the differential operator \(D_{j}\) by its action on \(f\)
\[
D_{j} f(\boldsymbol{x})
= \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f(\boldsymbol{x} + t\boldsymbol{e}_{j}) - f(\boldsymbol{x})}{t} = \frac{d}{dx_{j}}f(\boldsymbol{x}),
\]
whenever the limit exists. This is the partial derivative of \(f\) with respect to \(\boldsymbol{x}_{j}\).

\(D_{j}\) (or \(\frac{d}{d x_{j}}\)) is an operator that acts on functions,
\(\boldsymbol{e}_{j}\) is the \(j\)-th standard basis vector of \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\), and
\(\frac{d}{dx_{j}}f(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the result, itself a function evaluated at \(\boldsymbol{x}\).

Partial derivatives are thus special cases of directional derivatives. The directional derivative along direction \(\boldsymbol{v}\) is defined by the limit
\[
D_{\boldsymbol{v}} f(\boldsymbol{x})
= \lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f(\boldsymbol{x} + t\boldsymbol{v}) - f(\boldsymbol{x})}{t} = \left\langle df(\boldsymbol{x}), \boldsymbol{v}\right\rangle,
\]
where we assume \(\|\boldsymbol{v}\| = 1\) and the brackets \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) denote an inner product. There are a few things to note here:

Partial derivatives depend on your basis elements. Thus, partial derivatives depend on your choice of coordinate system.
Directional derivatives are anchored to directions. They are insensitive to coordinate systems.
Both partial and directional derivatives are scalars representing slopes of tangent lines.
The object \(df(\boldsymbol{x})\) is the first differential of \(f\).

A differential generalizes the notion of slope to more abstract objects. Specifically, it is the best linear approximation to a function based on the Taylor-like expansion
\[
f(\boldsymbol{x} + t\boldsymbol{v}) \approx f(\boldsymbol{x}) + \langle df(\boldsymbol{x}), (t \boldsymbol{v})\rangle.
\]
Indeed, when \(f\) is differentiable in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) the differential \(df(\boldsymbol{x})\) is unique and defines the gradient of \(f\)
\[
\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x}) = (D_{1}f(\boldsymbol{x}), D_{2}(\boldsymbol{x}), \ldots, D_{d}(\boldsymbol{x}))^{\top} = df((\boldsymbol{x}))^{\top}.
\]

title: Optimization Intro
text:
Differentation with abstract objects
On the surface, the language in our definitions appears entirely focused on vectors in the sense of 1D arrays. What we really require is some notion of inner product
\[
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle: V \times V \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
This is map taking two elements of a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) and assigning them a scalar from the underlying field (\(\mathbb{R}\) for our purposes). The outputs of inner products relate “magnitude” to “angles” between objects, and thus helps us define what it means to be “orthogonal”.
Examples:

Euclidean vector space with the “dot” product serving as inner product; i.e. \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\) and \(\langle \boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}\rangle = \boldsymbol{x} \cdot \boldsymbol{y} = \boldsymbol{x}^{\top} = \boldsymbol{y}\).
The set of \(m \times n\) matrices (is a vector space) with trace \(\mathrm{tr}(\cdot)\) serving as inner product; i.e. \(\boldsymbol{A}, \boldsymbol{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\) and \(\langle\boldsymbol{A},\boldsymbol{B}\rangle = \mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol{A}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B})\).
The set of square integrable functions with common domain \(\Omega\); i.e. \(f,g\) square integrable functions and \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_{\Omega} f(x) g(x) dx\).
The set of real-valued random variables with \(\langle X, Y \rangle = E[XY]\). See the previous example; need some measure theory to see this perspective.

title: Optimization Intro
section: Deriving the Normal Equations in Ordinary Regression
text:
Deriving the Normal Equations in Ordinary Regression
Compute the gradients of the following functions:

\(g(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \boldsymbol{X} \boldsymbol{\beta}\), where \(\boldsymbol{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}\).
\(h(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \boldsymbol{\beta}^{\top} \boldsymbol{C} \boldsymbol{\beta}\), where \(\boldsymbol{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\)
\(f(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \|\boldsymbol{y} - \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|^{2}\).

Use the stationary condition \(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \boldsymbol{0}\) to derive the normal equations.

title: Optimization Intro
text:
Normal Equations for Multivariate Regression
Now suppose you have a multivariate response \(\boldsymbol{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times c}\); rows are observations and columns correspond to components of the response. The objective function for constructing an estimator based on least squares is
\[
f(\boldsymbol{B}) = \|\boldsymbol{Y} - \boldsymbol{X}\boldsymbol{B}\|_{F}^{2},
\]
where the subscript \(F\) indicates the Frobenius norm. What is the gradient with respect to \(\boldsymbol{B} \in \mathbb{R}^{p \times c}\)? Use the stationary condition \(\nabla f(\boldsymbol{B}) = \boldsymbol{0}\) to derive the normal equations.

title: The File System
text:
Goals

Understand the organizational structure of a file system on Linux.
Understand relative and absolute paths.
Develop awareness of key locations on a Linux system and the class Docker image.
Understand that programs, regardless of operating system, operate in a context.

title: The File System
text:
Overview
Files on computers are generally arranged in a hierarchical manner, specifically as a rooted tree. The following is the output of tree -L 1 / on a machine with macOS Sequoia. This command displays a file system, one level deep, starting from the root directory /:
/
├── Applications
├── bin
├── cores
├── dev
├── etc -> private/etc
├── home -> /System/Volumes/Data/home
├── Library
├── opt
├── private
├── sbin
├── System
├── tmp -> private/tmp
├── Users
├── usr
├── var -> private/var
└── Volumes

17 directories, 0 files
Everything is a file in the Unix world, yet the output above clearly distinguishes between files and directories. Files are data on your computer. Directories are, too, but their role is to act as folders connecting one level of a tree to other parts in the system. In brief, directories are branches and files are leaves in the rooted tree structure.






ImportantSymbolic Links



You might notice a few of the labels in the tree output above have arrows; for example home -> /System/Volumes/Data/home. These are examples of symbolic links, which are files that point to a location elsewhere. Symbolic links are useful for introducing indirection and decoupling an interface from an implementation.

Indirection, as a concept, can be useful for creating shortcuts. For example, say you have multiple projects that need access to a particular resource nested deeply within your file system. A single symbolic link can provide access at a convenient location and allow each project to inherit access without writing out cumbersome paths.
To give another example, symbolic links can be used to manage versions of a resource. If two projects need access to two versions of FANCY_DATASET, each project can use its own symbolic link FANCY_DATASET which points to the appropriate version. This simplifies any scripts operating on that resource without having to introduce version information into the code.



The following is mock output of tree on a directory named repo. Your Git repository for this class will resemble this structure over time.
repo/
├── hw/
│   ├── hw1/
│   │   ├── complex_data.arrow
│   │   ├── fancy_algorithm.jl
│   │   ├── report.qmd
│   │   ├── Project.toml
│   │   └── <other code or files>
│   ├── hw2/
│   │
│   ...
│   └── hw8/
└── labs/
    ├── lab1/
    │   ├── report.qmd
    │   ├── Project.toml
    │   └── test.jl
    ...
    └── lab8
Here repo/ is the top level, so we can say these files are rooted at repo/, but it is not the root directory. The root directory is unique because Unix/Linux file systems are generally rooted trees. By definition, there can only be one root that serves as the absolute top level.

title: The File System
text:
Absolute vs Relative Paths
Virtually every operating system operates on file paths. A file path is a sequence of names/labels of specific files/directories in a file system that point to a specific location. On Linux, file paths are formatted by the file separator /. Let’s revisit the repo/ example:
repo/
├── hw/
│   ├── hw1/
│   │   ├── complex_data.arrow
│   │   ├── fancy_algorithm.jl
│   │   ├── report.qmd
│   │   ├── Project.toml
│   │   └── <other code or files>
│   ├── hw2/
...

The file path repo/ leads from wherever repo/ exists to repo/. Equivalently, ./repo.
The file path repo/hw is similar, but points one directory down towards hw/. Equivalently, ./repo/hw.
The file path repo/hw/hw1/report.qmd is a file path that leads from wherever repo/ exists to report.qmd. Equivalently, ./reop/hw/hw1/report.qmd.

All these examples are relative paths because they depend on context. That context is ., a symbolic file path that points here which is wherever you might be. From here you can reference the parent directory using .. which is whatever the parent might be.
In contrast, absolute paths do not depend on context because they’re absolute! On a Linux system, /repo/hw/hw1/report.qmd is an example of an absolute path (that probably does not exist). Let’s modify the example so that repo/ resides inside a stat206/ directory somewhere on the file system:
/
├──Documents
│   └──stat206
│       └── repo
...         ├── hw
            │   ├── hw1/
            │   │   ├── complex_data.arrow
            │   │   ├── fancy_algorithm.jl
            │   │   ├── report.qmd
            │   │   ├── Project.toml
            │   │   └── <other code or files>
            │   ├── hw2/
            ...
Here /Documents/stat206/repo/ is an absolute path that references repo. On Linux, all absolute paths must begin with the root directory, /. This eliminates any ambiguity.

Use in Programming and Data Analysis
In practice, we rarely, if ever, use absolute paths. Relative paths are preferred because two machines rarely share the same structure in their file systems. This is all the more relevant if we consider machines that have completely different operating systems. We conclude with the following advice that ought to ring true in many contexts.

Be thoughtful about how you organize files for a project. Stick to conventions, where possible, and aim for simplicity whenever guidance is scarce.
Prepend your file paths with . and .. to communicate your intent in references. It might help you or other catch mistakes.
Place scripts close to the top level of a project’s directory. This often simplifies relative paths.
Avoid hard-coding file separators into your code source files. Most programming languages provide tools to handle file separators correctly across operating systems.







ImportantAside: What about Windows?




There is no “root directory” in Windows, at least not in the same sense as Unix-like file systems. Windows file systems use drive letters as the root node; for example, the C:\ drive. Unix-like/Linux-like systems support working with multiple drives, too, but do not anchor their file systems to specific drives.
Windows uses the backslash \ as a file separator. It is one of the reasons (but not the only reason) we cannot hard-code file paths in scripts.

title: The File System
section: Special Locations on Linux File Systems
text:
Special Locations on Linux File Systems
Most operating systems exploit the hierarchical nature of file systems to organize sensitive information and tools so that permission settings can readily provide a level of security. The following are useful locations for you to be aware about:

/: The root directory. User accounts typically do not have file permissions here, and you should keep it that way.
/usr: Home to user-level resources. These are common to all users on a machine.

/usr/bin: Home to essential binaries, or programs, for the operating system. Commands like mv and cd exist here.
/usr/lib: Home to libraries required by applications. Can be source code, scripts, or compiled objects.

/etc: Home to system-wide configuration files.
/home: Contains the home directories for individual users. Your home directory on our Docker image is /home/student. Your shell sessions always start here.

~: Same as /home/${USERNAME}.

/var: A variable directory that holds files changing continuously during operation; for example, log files for applications can be found here under /var/log.
/tmp: A volatile workspace for temporary files. Treat it as a workspace, as systems are typically configured to periodically clean up (delete files) this workspace.


Our Docker Image
There are a few directories in the home directory /home/student that you should be aware of:

/home/student/.config: We will use this to store configuration files; for example, your Git identity.
/home/student/.ssh: We will use this to store keys for SSH authentication, mainly for GitHub.
/home/student/.local: We will use this to install software not included by default. No need for sudo!

Goals

Understand literate programming as a tool for communicating results from computational projects.
