title: Functions
text: Goals

title: Functions
text:
Overview
Functions are the basic units by which we assemble solutions to complex problems. This is especially true in R and Julia, as the languages strongly favor a Functional Programming (FP) style. These languages greatly benefit from ideas in other FP languages (e.g. Lisp) that came before and which evolved concurrently. One key aspect of FP is that functions are treated like any other object in the language (first-class citizens).






Note



For the Python users, the language favors a particular flavor of object-oriented programming that puts lets emphasis on functions/methods and more on classes. But functions remain important!

title: Functions
text:
Syntax and Semantics

function func(req1, req2; key1=dflt1, key2=dflt2)
  # do stuff
  return out1, out2, out3
end


Required arguments are separated by a comma and use positional notation.
Optional arguments need a default value in the signature.
Semicolons are not required in a function call. It is used to separate positional arguments from keyword arguments.
A return statement is optional, but highly encouraged in STAT 206.
If your function needs to return multiple values, use a Tuple, Dict, or NamedTuple.


Anonymous Functions
Anonymous functions are functions without a name.

These are short functions in terms of code length.
Used only once and have no reuse value.
Are commonly used in collection functions or list comprehensions.


Example: Squaring numbers in a collection

y = 1:9

Use an anonymous function for this straightforward calculation:

map(x -> x^2, y)

Better yet, the abs2() function does exactly what we need:

map(abs2, y)

Suppose abs2() does not exist. Our function is ^(x, 2), it is just the application of the Binary operator ^ with the second argument fixed to the value 2. The Base.Fix2 construct can help avoid anonymous functions:

map(Base.Fix2(^, 2), y) # use sparingly




Pass by sharing
In Julia, all arguments to functions are passed by sharing, in contrast to R and Matlab.






Important



Function names ending with ! indicate that the function mutates at least one argument, typically the first. This is strictly a convention; adding ! to the end of a Julia function does nothing semantically.

title: Functions
text:
Variable scope and rules
Variable scope and the associated rules defining scope are all about what functions can “see” and “do”.

Each function has its own environment, or local scope.
Names here override names in the global scope.
Internal environment starts with the named arguments.
If your computer encounters an undefined name in a function, it looks for it in the environment of the next outer scope where the function was defined. This is known as lexical scope.

Julia, R, and Python all use some variation of these rules for variable scope. That is, they all use lexical scope to resolve any “free” variables/symbols.
Julia’s scope rules are more or less straightforward. Below are some Julia-specific quirks:

Everything lives in the Main module, but default. It is the enclosing global scope for interactive environments; e.g. if you are working in the Julia REPL.
Global references must be declared using global for consistent behavior. Otherwise, global references will change depending on context, due to hard vs soft scoping.
Julia allows mutation of mutable types. This reason alone is a good reason to avoid global references at all costs.
Scalars are immutable, as are many other constructs. You cannot change their content.
An Array object is mutable, so changing the content of an Array instance persists outside a function call.
Remember that x = <expr> binds the RHS to the left; x .= <expr> fills the LHS with the RHS.







TipAvoid global variables!




Reduces risk of confusion and error.
Exception: Reserve global variables for true universal concepts like \(\pi\).
Exception: Allocating work buffers in large and sophisticated libraries like BLAS/LAPACK.




Example: Using a global variable

x = 7
y = ['A', 'C', 'G', 'T', 'U']

function adder(y)
  global x # specify a global reference
  x = x + y
  return x
end

Let’s see what happens to x and y when we call the function with a particular value.

adder(1)


x # oh the humanity!


y

Outside the adder() function:

x is a symbol that binds the scalar value 7.
y is a symbol that binds the specified Array value.

Inside the adder() function:

The symbol y is declared as a local variable; specifically it is the name of the first (and only) argument to the function.
The symbol x is declared as a global reference. We pull its value from the next outer scope.
Surprisingly, we manage to modify x but not y!



Example: Redefining π
In Julia, the symbols pi and π are defined in the language as convenient references to the number \(\pi\). While it is convenient to use, it is a global variable and therefore carries some risk.
The following function uses pi to compute the area of a circle with radius r:

circle_area(r) = pi*r^2

Check that is works as expected:

circle_area.([1, 2, 3])

What happens if we modify a global constant?

truepi = pi
pi = 3
circle_area.([1, 2, 3])


pi = truepi # restore sanity
circle_area.([1, 2, 3])

title: Functions
text:
Using functions

Nesting
Functions can be nested. In the example below, the outerfunction() can be invoked in the enclosing scope, whereas the innerfunction() is only visible within outerfunction().

function outerfunction()
  # do some outer stuff
  function innerfunction()
    # do inner stuff
    # can access prior outer definitions
  end
  # do more outer stuff
end







TipWhat’s the use case?



It is sometimes advantageous to hide helper functions where they are used, especially if they are not used elsewhere. Inner functions are also used to create closures, functions that “fix” some arguments to another function. We will discuss these at a later date.




Recursion
Julia supports recursive function definitions.
A successful recursive implementation of a function requires two key ingredients:

A base case. How do we know when to stop recursion?
A recursive step. How do we build the next item in the recursion?

Without a base case, a recursive function will create too many calls to itself and trigger a StackOverflow exception. This is a protection built into programming langauges to prevent “runaway code” that never terminates.

Example: Factorial
The following code implements the factorial function, \(n! = n \times (n-1) \times \ldots \times 2 \times 1\).

function myfactorial(n)
  if n > 1
    # recursive step
    return n * myfactorial(n-1)
  else
    # base case; treats x! = 1 for any x <= 0.
    return 1
  end
end


@show myfactorial(3)
@show myfactorial(6);




Vectorization
Scalar functions can be vectorized using the Dot (.) syntax:

# defined for scalar
function myfunc(x)
    return sin(x^2)
end


x = randn(5, 3)
myfunc.(x) # this is applied element-wise; always opt-in

Several levels of vectorization can be achieved using @.. In particular, this macro is a mechanism for loop fusion.

x = zeros(10)
y = randn(10)
display(y)
@. x = max(0, y) # vectorize `max()` AND `=`



Higher-order functions
Julia allows functions as arguments to other functions. You can even write functions to generate other functions.


List comprehensions

[sin(2i + j) for i in 1:5, j in 1:3] # similar to Python

title: Functions
text:
How to write (Julia) functions

Treat function signatures as interfaces
Interfaces are the inputs or arguments; the outputs or return value.

An interface tells the caller what is required.
Outside perspective: Try to avoid caring about what is inside a function or how it carries out its work.

Calls other functions: ifelse(), abs(), operators ^ and >, and could also call other functions we’ve written.
Keep the internals orthogonal to the external; that’s encapsulation.

return says what the output is; alternately, return the last evaluation.

We often do not need to care about this; just use return to be explicit!

Comments: Not required but a good idea.

Helps document what kinds of inputs are required.
Julia and R are dynamic languages. No constructs to enforce types in signatures.
Documentation/comments should signal what is/isn’t allowed.




What should be a function?

Things you’re going to re-run, especially if it will be re-run with changes.
Chunks of code you keep highlighting and hitting return on.
Chunks of code which are small parts of a larger analysis or process.
Chunks of code which are very similar to other chunks.



Named and default arguments
Consider the “robust” loss function
\[
\psi(x) = \begin{cases}
  2 |x| - 1, & x^{2} > 1 \\
  x^{2}, & x^{2} \le 1
\end{cases}.
\]
We define two versions of this function below:

# Robust loss function for outlier-resistant regression
# Inputs: vector of numbers (x)
# Outputs: vector with x^2 for small entries, |x| for large ones
function psi1(x)
  psi = ifelse(x^2 > 1, 2*abs(x) - 1, x^2
  return psi
end

# Robust loss function for outlier-resistant regression
# Inputs: vector of numbers (x), scale for crossover (c)
# Outputs: vector with x^2 for small entries, 2c|x|-c^2 for large ones
function psi2(x; c::Reall = 1.0)
  psi = ifelse(x^2 > c^2, 2*c*abs(x) - c^2, x^2)
  return psi
end

Let’s check that they are the same when \(c=1\):

z = 1.3
psi1(z) ≈ psi2(z; c = 1.0)

Notice that default values are used whenever named arguments are missing:

psi2(z; c = 1.0) ≈ psi2(z)

Julia enforces order in positional arguments due to its multiple dispatch system. Can’t mimic what you see on the R side for shuffling arguments.


Checking arguments
Problem: We see odd behavior when arguments are not specified as expected.

psi2(z; c = Float64[1, 1, 1, 10])

Solution: Put sanity checks in the code. Ideally, put any input validation at the top of the function body.

function psi3(x; c::Real = 1)
  if !(c isa Number)
    error("Parameter `c` should be given as a number. Did you mean `psi3.(x; c = c)`?)")
  elseif c < 0
    error("Parameter `c` should be positive. Got $(c).")
  end
  return psi2(x; c = c) # now this is safe!
end

The error() function will stop execution and allow you to pass an informative message to a user. Can also throw() more specific errors; e.g. throw(DomainError(...)) or @assert some_condition.

psi3(z; c = -1.0)



Encapsulation: Respect the interfaces!

Interfaces mark out a controlled environment for our code.
A function interacts with the rest of a system only at the interface.
Similarly, the “output” should only be through the return value.

That means avoiding side-effects, which are modifications to some external state not defined inside a function.


Your goal in writing a function is to achieve encapsulation: separate what your function does from how it implements its task.

It should do one and only one thing as well as possible.
If your function needs to modify some state/data, then that state/data ought to be arguments to the function.
Information that is unrelated to what a function does should be minimized as much as possible.

title: Use Revise.jl
text:
Goals

Install Revise.jl in your main Julia environment.
Integrate Revise.jl into your workflow: you’ll never have to to re-run code chunks again.

title: Use Revise.jl
text:
Motivation
If you’ve ever worked with R Markdown, Quarto Markdown, or Jupyter notebooks, then you are likely familiar with the following workflow:

Write some code, maybe across several code chunks/cells.
Realize there is an error in a function defined in chunk 8.
Edit the code in chunk 8.
Go back to chunk 20 and re-run it. Nothing changed?!
Oh, we forgot to run chunk 8 again. Done.
Huh, does anything else in my notebook depend on that function?

These systems are fantastic when writing brief chunks of code, particularly in illustrating a specific point to the reader. It is difficult, and in fact impossible, to write more elaborate code approaching the complexity of a library/package.
Most of the work you’ll be doing in this class is better handled in code source files (.jl for Julia), with Quarto Markdown reserved for documenting your thought process and communicating results. Yet, that does not quite solve the issue mentioned above as the workflow now becomes:

Open a Julia REPL (perhaps connected to a Quarto document)
Load source files with include("mycode.jl").
Experiment and discover an issue.
Fix the issue, then reload source files with include("mycode.jl").
Wait, it was actually include("other_source.jl")…

The Revise.jl package in Julia was designed to avoid this problem, easing the cognitive load on developers by keeping the focus on iterative development.

title: Use Revise.jl
text:
How do we install it?
To get the most out of Revise.jl, you’ll want to install it in your “global” or “main” environment. In a Julia REPL, you can check by typing ] to enter Package mode:
Julia mode (default):
julia>
Package mode:
(@v1.12) pkg>
If you do not see (@v1.12) in the prompt, type activate + Enter while in Package mode to activate the global environment for Julia 1.12. Finally, we can install the package by running the command
(@v1.12) pkg> add Revise
After some work in the background, you’ll have the package available for any of your projects in this class.

title: Use Revise.jl
text:
How do we use it?

Loading Revise.jl
First, we need to load it like any other Julia package:
using Revise
Critically, we need to do this before loading any packages or source files!


Hooking into Revise.jl

Create a Julia source file for your work (if you do not have one already). Let’s say we’re working on mysource.jl.
Load the source code using includet("mysource.jl"). The t is not a typo!

… and that’s it. Now, any changes you make to mysource.jl will automatically be reflected in your Julia session.

title: Use Revise.jl
text:
Frequently Asked Questions

What can Revise track?
See the Revise documentation on this topic. Short answer: virtually anything you might care about in this class.


Revise isn’t working! What gives?
Has the Julia prompt changed from green to yellow? If so, that means Revise.jl encountered an error trying to propagate your edits to source code somewhere. Try running:

Revise.errors() to check any error messages that you may have missed.
Revise.retry() to force Revise.jl to propagate changes again.
Revise.duplicate_methods() to see if the error is due to duplicated method definitions in your code.

title: Submit Assignments
text:
Solutions to lab and homework assignments will consist of several files.

Quarto Markdown. Your main report must be prepared using Quarto Markdown (.qmd) source files. Other formats, such as Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) will not be accepted. These files combine code, code outputs, and explanatory texts to answer problem prompts.
Project.toml. Each assignment is a mini-project with its own computing environment. You must carefully manage that environment using Julia’s package manager to specify each dependency (both in the standard library and from the package ecosystem).
Julia Source. Later in the course, your solutions will involve code spanning several lines, multiple functions, custom types, and possibly custom modules. These must be defined in separate Julia source files (.jl).
Inputs and Outputs. Some assignments will require external data and generate outputs, such as data subsets, summary tables, benchmarking results, or graphics. These must be included as part of your submissions.

You will use Git to version control these files and upload your work to a remote repository on GitHub.

Provide a central hub for a Git repository.

Share your work with others, or backup your local workspaces remotely.

Both private and public options.
GitHub provides a few incentives for users with EDU email addresses.
Can also be used to create a personal website.
